subject: ss
title: Government in Action: Elections, Parties, Interest Groups, and Lawmaking
objectives: You will explain how the Electoral College works, calculate a state's electoral votes, and find the winner of an election from a results table.
You will describe what political parties and interest groups do and tell the two apart.
You will trace the path of a bill through Congress to the president, including vetoes, overrides, and pocket vetoes, using the text of Article I, Section 7.
You will identify the five stages of public policy and show how all three branches take part after a law is passed.
You will answer GED-style questions using constitutional excerpts, election tables, charts, and described political cartoons.

slides.title: Government in Action
slides.board:
Week 4 Social Studies: Government in Action

Today you will:

  • Explain the Electoral College and find the winner from a results table
  • Tell political parties and interest groups apart
  • Trace a bill through Congress to the president, including vetoes and overrides
  • Name the stages of public policy and the role of each branch
  • Answer GED questions with excerpts, tables, charts, and cartoons

Plan: Warm-up → four big ideas → we do it together → you do it → GED questions

notes.say: Last week we studied the rights the Constitution protects. This week we watch the government actually work: how leaders are chosen, how groups try to shape what government does, and how an idea becomes a law and then a program. Civics and government are about half of the GED Social Studies test, and these topics show up as results tables, excerpts from Article I, charts, and cartoons. One ground rule: we study how the system works, not who should win. Every election table today uses fictional candidates on purpose.
ask: When people vote for president in November, are they voting directly for the president? (Expected: most students say yes. Do not correct it yet; tell them we will come back to it in ten minutes.)
notes.watch: Keep the lesson nonpartisan. If the student starts debating a current party or candidate, redirect: "Good conversation for later. For the GED, what does the document or table say?"

slides.title: Warm-up: Week 3 Review
slides.board:
Answer each one.

  1. Which amendment protects freedom of speech, press, religion, assembly, and the right to petition the government?
  2. Each amendment kept states from denying the vote for one reason. What reason does each cover? (a) 15th (b) 19th (c) 26th
  3. Civil liberty or civil right? (a) A city may not jail a reporter for criticizing the mayor. (b) A restaurant may not refuse to serve customers because of their race.
  4. Required or voluntary for citizens? (a) voting (b) serving on a jury when summoned
steps: 1. The First Amendment. Keep "petition" in mind: it is the right interest groups use today.
2. (a) 15th: race (1870). (b) 19th: sex, so women can vote (1920). (c) 26th: age, voting at 18 (1971).
3. (a) Civil liberty: a freedom the government may not take away (free press). (b) Civil right: equal treatment, no discrimination.
4. (a) Voting is voluntary, though it is one of the most important things a citizen does. (b) Jury service when summoned is required.

notes.say: These four questions review last week and set up this week. The First Amendment's right "to petition the Government" is the legal root of lobbying, and the voting amendments decide who takes part in the elections we study today. Give the student about three minutes, have them say each answer, then reveal. If they miss the civil liberty/civil right pair, repeat the short version: liberties are freedoms from government; rights are equal treatment.
ask: Which amendment lowered the voting age to 18? (Expected: the 26th)
What is the difference between a civil liberty and a civil right? (Expected: a liberty is a freedom government cannot take away; a right is equal treatment under the law)
notes.answer: 1. First Amendment. 2. (a) race, (b) sex, (c) age 18. 3. (a) civil liberty, (b) civil right. 4. (a) voluntary, (b) required.
notes.watch: Students often say voting is required. It is a responsibility and a right, but no federal law requires a citizen to vote. Jury service, taxes, and obeying laws are required.

slides.title: Two Rounds: Primaries and the General Election
slides.board:
Round 1: Primary or caucus picks each party's nominee.
Closed primary = only that party's registered voters. Open primary = any registered voter picks one party's ballot.
Round 2: General election picks the winner (Tuesday after the first Monday in November).

OfficeHow manyTerm
Representative4352 years
Senator100 (2 per state)6 years; about 1/3 elected every 2 years
President14 years; two-term limit (22nd Amendment, 1951)

notes.say: Most American elections happen in two rounds. First the parties choose their candidates in a primary election or a caucus, which is a meeting of party members. In a closed primary only voters registered with that party can take part; in an open primary any registered voter can choose one party's ballot. Then the general election decides who actually holds the office. Because the whole House and a third of the Senate are elected every two years, the elections in the middle of a president's term, called midterm elections, can change who controls Congress. Senators have been elected directly by the voters since the 17th Amendment in 1913, which we saw last week.
ask: Why is about one-third of the Senate elected every two years instead of all 100 at once? (Expected: senators serve 6-year terms that are staggered, so 6 ÷ 2 = 3 groups)
What does a primary decide, and what does a general election decide? (Expected: the party's nominee; who wins the office)
notes.watch: Students mix up "primary" and "general." Use the sports picture: the primary is the playoff inside each party; the general election is the championship between the parties' nominees.

slides.title: The Electoral College
slides.board:
A state's electoral votes = its House members + 2 senators
District of Columbia = 3 (23rd Amendment)
Total: 435 + 100 + 3 = 538    To win: a majority = 270

  • Winner-take-all: in 48 states and D.C., the statewide winner gets all of that state's electoral votes.
  • House seats, and so electoral votes, shift with the census every 10 years.
  • No one reaches 270? The House chooses from the top three; each state delegation casts one vote (12th Amendment).

notes.say: Here is the answer to the opening question. In November, voters in each state are really choosing a slate of electors, and the electors cast the official votes for president. Article II of the Constitution gives each state as many electors as it has members of Congress. Every state has two senators, so even the smallest state has at least three electoral votes. Nearly every state is winner-take-all: winning a state by one vote earns the same electoral votes as winning it by a million. Only Maine and Nebraska can split their votes by district. That is why a candidate can win the most votes nationwide and still lose; it is usually counted as happening five times: 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016.
ask: Where does 538 come from? (Expected: 435 representatives + 100 senators + 3 for D.C.)
Why is 270 the magic number and not 269? (Expected: half of 538 is 269, which would be a tie; a majority must be more than half)
notes.watch: Students sometimes add 2 to the number of senators or forget D.C. Have them say the formula out loud: "House plus two."

slides.title: Worked Example: Counting Electoral Votes
slides.board:
1. A state has 9 members in the House. How many electoral votes does it have?
  2. A state has 28 electoral votes. How many House members does it have?
  3. What is the smallest number of electoral votes any state can have, and why?
steps: 1. House members + 2 senators: 9 + 2 = 11 electoral votes.
2. Work backward: electoral votes − 2 senators: 28 − 2 = 26 House members.
3. Every state has at least 1 House member and always 2 senators: 1 + 2 = 3.
Check: a candidate who wins a 3-vote state and an 11-vote state has 14 of the 270 needed.

notes.say: Model the formula out loud each time: "House plus two." Then show that the formula works backward too, because the GED sometimes gives the electoral votes and asks about House seats. The third question explains why small states always have at least three: the two Senate seats are guaranteed no matter how few people live there.
ask: If a state gains one House seat after the census, what happens to its electoral votes? (Expected: they go up by one)
notes.watch: On question 2, some students add 2 instead of subtracting (answer 30). Ask: "Are the senators already inside the 28, or not yet?"

slides.title: Worked Example: Who Wins?
slides.board:
A fictional country uses winner-take-all electoral votes.

StateElectoral votesLeeMoss
Alpha9600,000400,000
Beta7300,000320,000
Gamma5200,000230,000

Who wins the electoral vote? Who wins the popular vote?
steps: Step 1: Majority needed. 9 + 7 + 5 = 21 electoral votes. More than half of 21 is 11.
Step 2: State winners. Alpha: Lee (600,000 > 400,000). Beta: Moss (320,000 > 300,000). Gamma: Moss (230,000 > 200,000).
Step 3: Electoral votes. Lee: 9. Moss: 7 + 5 = 12. Moss reaches 11, so Moss wins.
Step 4: Popular votes. Lee: 600,000 + 300,000 + 200,000 = 1,100,000. Moss: 400,000 + 320,000 + 230,000 = 950,000. Lee wins the popular vote by 150,000 but loses the election.

notes.say: This is the most common table question on the GED, so model the order carefully: majority first, then each state's winner, then add electoral votes only, then popular votes only if the question asks. Point out why the result happened: Lee's big 200,000-vote margin in Alpha earned no extra electoral votes, while Moss won two states by small margins.
ask: Which state's result explains why Lee lost even with more votes? (Expected: Alpha, where Lee's large margin was "wasted" because winner-take-all gives no extra credit)
notes.watch: The classic mistake is adding the popular votes first and declaring Lee the winner. Make the student write the state winner's name next to each row before doing any addition.

In which state did Tate get "wasted" votes? (Expected: Oak, won by 180,000)

slides.title: Political Parties
slides.board:
Political party: an organization that nominates candidates and tries to win elections to control government.

  • Nominate candidates (their most important job)
  • Write a platform (goals; each goal is a "plank")
  • Inform voters and get them to the polls
  • Organize government: Speaker of the House and Senate majority leader are chosen through the parties

Two-party system: one winner per district makes it hard for third parties to win, but their ideas often get adopted.

notes.say: Parties are not mentioned in the Constitution. George Washington warned against "the spirit of party" in his Farewell Address in 1796, yet the first parties formed in the 1790s around Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson. Today's two major parties are the Democratic Party and the Republican Party, which was founded in 1854. Why only two? Most U.S. elections give the seat to whoever gets the most votes in a district, so a smaller party that finishes second or third everywhere wins nothing. Ross Perot, an independent, won about 19 percent of the popular vote in 1992 and zero electoral votes. Still, third parties matter: the Populist Party of the 1890s pushed for electing senators directly, which became the 17th Amendment.
ask: What is a party's most important job? (Expected: nominating candidates)
Why do third parties rarely win? (Expected: one winner per district and winner-take-all; second place gets nothing)
notes.watch: Students may think parties are part of the government. They are private organizations; they organize the people who run the government.

slides.title: Interest Groups and the One-Question Test
slides.board:
Interest group: people with a shared goal who try to influence public policy without running their own candidates.

Types: business groups, labor unions, professional associations, single-issue and public-interest groups

Methods: lobbying · testifying at hearings · petitions · advertising · lawsuits · money through PACs

Test: Does the group nominate its own candidates to win control of government? Yes = party. No, it only tries to influence decisions = interest group.

notes.say: An interest group wants government to do something, or stop doing something, but it does not try to run the government itself. Lobbying means contacting officials to persuade them, and it is protected by the First Amendment right "to petition the Government" that we reviewed in the warm-up. Groups also testify at hearings, run ads, file lawsuits, and raise money through political action committees, or PACs, which give to candidates. Here is the trap: an interest group may endorse candidates or give them money and still be an interest group. The question is whether it nominates its own candidates to take control of government.
ask: A labor union's PAC gives money to candidates from both major parties. Party or interest group? (Expected: interest group; giving money is not nominating)
notes.watch: Students see "supports candidates" and jump to "party." Make them apply the test word for word: nominate its own candidates?

slides.title: Worked Example: Party or Interest Group?
slides.board:
1. The Coastline Party holds a convention, adopts a platform, and nominates a candidate for governor.
  2. The Builders Alliance meets with state senators about a housing bill and gives money to candidates through its PAC.
  3. The Riverbend Parents Network endorses two school board candidates and asks members to vote for them. It nominates no one.
steps: 1. Political party. It nominates its own candidate and writes a platform to win control of the governor's office.
2. Interest group. Meeting senators is lobbying; PAC money is support, not a nomination.
3. Interest group. An endorsement backs someone else's candidate. The network does not nominate its own.
Rule: nominating = party. Lobbying, testifying, endorsing, donating, suing = interest group activity.

notes.say: Walk through the test on each case: does the group nominate its own candidates to win control of government? Case 3 is the hard one and the one the GED likes: endorsing candidates feels like party work, but the network is backing candidates who were nominated by someone else.
ask: Which word in case 1 settles it? (Expected: "nominates")
notes.watch: If the student labels case 3 a party, ask: "Whose candidates are these? Did the network choose them as its nominees?"

slides.title: We Do: Name the Group and the Method
slides.board:
Party or interest group? Then name the method.

  1. A retired teachers' association testifies before a House committee about pensions.
  2. A farm association's PAC donates to candidates in both major parties.
  3. A clean-water group sues a federal agency, saying it ignored a pollution law.
  4. The Liberty Coast Party asks voters in its primary to choose its nominee for the U.S. Senate.
steps: 1. Interest group: testifying at a hearing.
2. Interest group: campaign money through a PAC.
3. Interest group: a lawsuit (using the courts).
4. Political party: nominating a candidate through a primary.

notes.say: The student answers each one aloud, naming both the type of group and the method, before you reveal. Point out that number 3 shows interest groups can work through the judicial branch, not just Congress. The variety of methods is exactly what GED questions ask about.
ask: Which of the four uses a different branch of government from the others? (Expected: number 3, the lawsuit uses the courts)
notes.answer: 1. Interest group, testimony. 2. Interest group, PAC donations. 3. Interest group, lawsuit. 4. Party, nominating through a primary.

slides.title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
slides.board:
1. Introduce: only a member of Congress can. Tax (revenue) bills must start in the House.
  2. Committee: hearings and markup. Most bills die here.
  3. Floor: debate and a majority vote. Senate filibuster can block a vote; cloture takes 3/5 = 60 senators.
  4. Other chamber: must pass the identical text (conference committee if needed).
  5. President: signs or vetoes.

notes.say: Anyone can suggest a bill, including citizens, interest groups, or the president, but only a senator or representative can introduce it. The bill goes to a committee, often a subcommittee first, which holds hearings and marks it up, meaning it revises the text. Most bills never get out of committee. On the floor, the House limits debate through its Rules Committee. The Senate allows longer debate, so a senator can filibuster to block a vote; ending debate on most bills takes three-fifths of the Senate, 60 votes when every seat is filled. Passing the bill itself still takes only a simple majority. Then both chambers must agree on exactly the same words before the president sees it.
ask: Who can introduce a bill? (Expected: only a member of Congress)
Fifty-eight senators vote to end a filibuster. What happens? (Expected: debate continues; cloture needs 60)
notes.watch: Students confuse the 60 votes for cloture with the vote to pass a bill. Passing takes a simple majority; 60 is only to end debate.

slides.title: The President's Four Outcomes
slides.board:
The president…Result
signs the billLaw
vetoes it (returns it with objections)Dies, unless 2/3 of the House AND 2/3 of the Senate override
does nothing for 10 days (Sundays excepted), Congress still meetingLaw without a signature
does nothing, and Congress adjourns before the 10 days endDies: pocket veto

Source: Article I, Section 7

notes.say: All four outcomes come straight from Article I, Section 7 of the Constitution, so the GED can quote the text and ask you to apply it. The veto is the president's check on Congress, and the override is Congress's check back. An override needs two-thirds in both chambers; one chamber alone does nothing. The two "do nothing" rows look alike, so focus on one fact: is Congress still meeting? If yes, the bill becomes law. If Congress has adjourned and the president cannot return the bill, it dies, and that is a pocket veto. A pocket veto cannot be overridden, because nothing was returned for Congress to vote on.
ask: What one fact decides between "law without signature" and "pocket veto"? (Expected: whether Congress has adjourned)
Can Congress override a pocket veto? (Expected: no; it would have to pass the bill again from the start)
notes.watch: Students often think "doing nothing" always kills a bill. Point to the text: "the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it."

slides.title: Worked Example: Override Math
slides.board:
The president vetoes a bill. Every member votes.

  • House (435 members): 300 vote to override
  • Senate (100 members): 64 vote to override

Is the veto overridden?
steps: House needs: 2/3 × 435 = 290. It got 300. 300 ≥ 290, so the House succeeds.
Senate needs: 2/3 × 100 = 66.67, so 67 votes (you cannot cast part of a vote). It got 64. Senate fails.
Both chambers needed: the Senate fell short, so the veto stands and the bill does not become law.

notes.say: Show the math line by line: multiply by two-thirds, round up to the next whole vote if needed, then compare. The House part succeeds, which tempts students to say the bill becomes law. Stress that the override is like a door with two locks: both chambers must reach two-thirds. These counts assume every member votes, which is how GED problems usually set it up.
ask: How many senators would have had to switch for the override to pass? (Expected: 3, from 64 to 67)
notes.watch: Two mistakes: rounding 66.67 down to 66, and stopping after the House succeeds. Have the student write "2/3 + 2/3" next to every override question.

slides.title: Worked Example: Reading Article I, Section 7
slides.board:
"If any Bill shall not be returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him, the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it, unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law."

Congress keeps meeting all month. The president neither signs nor returns a bill for 10 days, not counting Sundays. What happens?
steps: Split the sentence into two cases. Case 1: not returned in 10 days → "shall be a Law." Case 2: "unless" Congress adjourned and prevented the return → "shall not be a Law."
Match the facts. Congress is still meeting, so nothing prevented the return. This is Case 1.
Answer: the bill becomes law without the president's signature.
Flip it: if Congress had adjourned after 4 days and the bill was unsigned, it would be Case 2, a pocket veto.

notes.say: Old documents pack two rules into one long sentence. Teach the student to find the turning word, here "unless," and split the sentence into an if-then for each case. Then match the facts of the question to one case. This habit works on every constitutional excerpt the GED gives.
ask: Which word turns the sentence from one case to the other? (Expected: "unless")
What does "Sundays excepted" mean? (Expected: Sundays are not counted in the 10 days)
notes.watch: Students who stop reading at "shall be a Law" miss the pocket veto entirely. Make them read every sentence to its final period.

slides.title: We Do: What Happens Next?
slides.board:
1. The House passes a highway bill. The Senate passes a version with different spending amounts. What must happen before the bill goes to the president?
  2. A senator talks for hours to block a vote. Then 58 senators vote to end debate. What happens?
  3. A senator wants to introduce a bill to raise income tax rates in the Senate first. Can she?
steps: 1. The differences must be settled (for example, by a conference committee), and both chambers pass the identical final version.
2. Debate continues. Cloture needs 60 votes when all seats are filled; 58 is not enough, so the filibuster goes on.
3. No. "All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives." The Senate may amend a revenue bill, but it must begin in the House.

notes.say: Each of these tests one rule from the flowchart. Have the student name the rule before giving the answer: "identical text," "60 for cloture," "revenue starts in the House." Point out that the Senate still has a say on tax bills: it can propose amendments once the House has started them.
ask: In number 2, how many more votes were needed? (Expected: 2)
notes.answer: 1. Settle the differences and pass identical versions in both chambers. 2. The filibuster continues; 60 votes needed for cloture. 3. No; revenue bills must start in the House.

slides.title: Public Policy and the Branches in Action
slides.board:
Public policy = what government decides to do (or not do) about a public problem.

Agenda setting → Formulation → Adoption → Implementation → Evaluation

BranchAfter a law passes, it…
Executivecarries it out; agencies write regulations
Judicialdecides cases; can rule a law unconstitutional (judicial review)
Legislativefunds it (power of the purse), holds oversight hearings; Senate confirms nominees

notes.say: Passing a law is the middle of the story, not the end. First a problem gets attention, which is agenda setting. Officials develop options, which is formulation. A law or decision is approved, which is adoption. Agencies carry it out, which is implementation, and later someone checks whether it worked, which is evaluation. For example, the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 created OSHA, an executive agency that writes and enforces workplace safety rules. Courts can strike down a law that violates the Constitution, a power established in Marbury v. Madison in 1803. Congress keeps watch by controlling the money and holding hearings.
ask: An agency writes detailed rules to carry out a new law. Which branch and which stage? (Expected: executive; implementation)
What is the stage right after implementation? (Expected: evaluation)
notes.watch: Students confuse formulation (developing options) with adoption (voting to approve one). Ask: "Has anyone voted yet?" If no, it is still formulation.

slides.title: Worked Example: The Scooter Problem
slides.board:
Fictional Brightwater:

  1. Hospital reports and news stories about e-scooter crashes lead the city council to discuss the problem.
  2. Council staff draft three options: a helmet rule, a 15-mph speed cap, or a downtown ban.
  3. The council votes 6–1 for the speed cap.
  4. The transportation department posts signs, and police begin enforcing the cap.
  5. A year later, the city reports scooter crashes fell by one-third.

Label each event with its policy stage.
steps: 1. Agenda setting: the problem gets officials' attention.
2. Formulation: options are developed and compared. No vote yet.
3. Adoption: the council approves one option.
4. Implementation: executive departments carry it out.
5. Evaluation: officials measure whether it worked.

notes.say: The five events are in order on purpose, so the student can see the whole cycle once. On the GED the events are often mixed up or only one is described, so teach the clue words: attention or complaints means agenda setting; options, studies, or drafts means formulation; vote or approve means adoption; carry out, enforce, build, or hire means implementation; report, study results, or measure means evaluation.
ask: Which clue word in event 3 tells you it is adoption? (Expected: "votes")
notes.watch: Event 5 says crashes fell, but the student should not conclude the speed cap caused the drop without more evidence. Evaluation measures results; proving cause takes comparison.

slides.title: We Do: Which Branch Is Acting?
slides.board:
Congress passes a clean-air law. Name the branch for each action.

  1. The Environmental Protection Agency writes detailed limits for factory smoke.
  2. A Senate committee holds a hearing and asks the agency head why the rules are late.
  3. A federal court rules that one part of the law violates the Constitution.
  4. Congress votes to cut the agency's budget for the program.
steps: 1. Executive: an agency writing regulations (implementation).
2. Legislative: an oversight hearing.
3. Judicial: judicial review.
4. Legislative: the power of the purse.

notes.say: This slide shows checks and balances after a law is passed. The executive branch carries it out, the courts can check it, and Congress keeps control through hearings and money. Have the student name the branch and the power each time.
ask: Which two actions are Congress checking the executive branch? (Expected: 2 and 4)
notes.answer: 1. Executive. 2. Legislative (oversight). 3. Judicial (judicial review). 4. Legislative (power of the purse).
notes.watch: Students may call the EPA part of Congress because it carries out a law Congress passed. Agencies are part of the executive branch.

slides.title: You Do 1: Elections and the Electoral College
slides.board:
On your own (4 minutes).

  1. A state has 5 House members. How many electoral votes does it have?
  2. A country has three states: X (10 electoral votes), Y (6), and Z (5). Candidate A wins X by 1 vote. Candidate B wins Y and Z by large margins. Who wins the electoral vote?
  3. What is the difference between a closed primary and an open primary?
  4. No candidate wins 270 electoral votes. Who chooses the president, and how many votes does each state get?
steps: 1. 5 + 2 = 7.
2. Total 21, majority 11. A has 10; B has 6 + 5 = 11. Candidate B wins.
3. Closed: only voters registered with that party. Open: any registered voter may choose one party's ballot.
4. The House of Representatives; each state's delegation casts one vote.

notes.say: Start a four-minute timer and stay quiet. When time is up, have the student give all four answers before you reveal any. On number 2, ask them to show the majority first. If they miss number 4, go back to the Electoral College slide.
ask: In number 2, did the size of A's win in X matter? (Expected: no; winner-take-all gives the same 10 votes for a 1-vote win)
notes.answer: 1. 7. 2. Candidate B, 11 to 10. 3. Closed: party members only; open: any registered voter. 4. The House; one vote per state delegation.

slides.title: You Do 2: Parties and Interest Groups
slides.board:
On your own (3 minutes).

  1. What is the most important job of a political party?
  2. A nurses' association meets with members of Congress about hospital staffing. It runs no candidates. Party or interest group? Which method is it using?
  3. What is a PAC?
  4. Give one reason third-party candidates rarely win.
steps: 1. Nominating candidates for office.
2. Interest group, using lobbying.
3. A political action committee: it raises money and gives it to candidates, often for an interest group.
4. Most elections have one winner per district (and winner-take-all electoral votes), so second or third place wins nothing.

notes.say: Three minutes on the timer. These are short recall and apply questions. When you check number 2, ask for the proof: "runs no candidates" settles that it is an interest group, and "meets with members of Congress" is lobbying.
notes.answer: 1. Nominating candidates. 2. Interest group; lobbying. 3. Political action committee, which gives money to candidates. 4. One winner per district / winner-take-all.

slides.title: You Do 3: Lawmaking and Policy
slides.board:
On your own (4 minutes).

  1. Every member votes on overriding a veto. House: 280 of 435 vote yes. Senate: 70 of 100 vote yes. Is the veto overridden?
  2. Congress adjourns 4 days after the president receives a bill. The president never signs it. What happens?
  3. A state agency studies whether a new seat-belt law reduced traffic deaths. Which policy stage is this?
  4. Which branch writes regulations to carry out a law?
steps: 1. No. House needs 290 (280 is short). The Senate's 70 ≥ 67 does not matter; both are needed.
2. The bill dies: a pocket veto.
3. Evaluation.
4. The executive branch (its agencies).

notes.say: Four minutes. Number 1 reverses the worked example: this time the Senate succeeds and the House fails. Ask the student to show 2/3 × 435 = 290 before answering. On number 2, have them name the deciding fact: Congress adjourned.
notes.answer: 1. No; the House fell short of 290. 2. Pocket veto; the bill dies. 3. Evaluation. 4. Executive.
notes.watch: If the student says yes on number 1 because the Senate passed two-thirds, return to the "two locks" picture.

slides.title: GED Question 1: A Constitutional Excerpt
slides.board:
"If any Bill shall not be returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him, the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it, unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law." (Article I, Section 7)

Congress sends a bill to the president on June 10 and adjourns for the year on June 13. The president does not sign it. What happens?

A. It becomes law after ten days without a signature.
B. It does not become law, because Congress's adjournment prevented its return.
C. Congress may override it with a two-thirds vote when it returns.
D. It goes to the Supreme Court to decide whether it becomes law.
steps: Eliminate A. That is Case 1, which applies only while Congress is still meeting. Here Congress adjourned after 3 days.
Eliminate C. An override is a response to a returned veto. Nothing was returned, so there is nothing to override.
Eliminate D. The excerpt never mentions the courts; this is outside information the text does not support.
Answer B. "unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law." This is a pocket veto.

notes.say: Let the student choose first, then eliminate out loud with a reason for each. A is the most tempting because it quotes the first half of the sentence. That is exactly how the GED builds a distractor: true for a different set of facts.
ask: Which date fact decides the answer? (Expected: Congress adjourned on June 13, before the 10 days were up)
notes.answer: B. The bill does not become law (pocket veto).
notes.watch: Students who choose A stopped reading at "shall be a Law." Have them put a finger on "unless."

slides.board:

Which conclusion is supported by the table?

A. California has more electoral votes per person than Wyoming.

notes.say: Data questions have three classic traps: reversing the relationship, mixing in a wrong fact, and predicting beyond the data. Ask the student to explain why the small state comes out ahead: the two Senate electoral votes go to every state no matter its size, so they count for more in a small state.
ask: Why does each Wyoming electoral vote represent fewer people? (Expected: every state gets 2 electoral votes for its senators regardless of population)
notes.answer: B. Each electoral vote in Wyoming represents fewer people than each one in California.
notes.watch: "Per person" and "people per vote" are opposites. If the student picks A, write both ratios side by side.

slides.title: GED Strategy: Turn the Rule Into Steps
slides.board:
Results table:

  1. Find the majority needed.
  2. Write each state's winner.
  3. Add electoral votes only.
  4. Look at popular votes only if asked.

Constitutional excerpt:

  1. Find the turning word (unless, but, if).
  2. Split the sentence into if…then cases.
  3. Match the question's facts to one case.

Pace: about 2 minutes per question on our practice tests.

notes.say: The questions in this topic look different from each other, but they all hand you a rule and a set of facts. The fastest, safest approach is to turn the rule into a short checklist and run the facts through it in order. Students who skip steps on tables end up adding popular votes, and students who skip the turning word on excerpts miss the exception. Writing the steps takes ten seconds and saves the question.
ask: What is the first thing you do with an electoral results table? (Expected: find the majority needed)
notes.watch: Strong readers sometimes answer from memory instead of the excerpt. Ask: "Which words in the excerpt prove that?"

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
The Constitution sets up the government. Elections, political parties, interest groups, and the lawmaking process are how that government actually works from day to day. GED Social Studies questions on these topics usually hand you a results table, a chart, a piece of the Constitution, or a described cartoon, and ask you to figure out what it shows or what happens next.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Explain how the Electoral College works, count a state's electoral votes, and find the winner from a results table
  • Describe what political parties and interest groups do, and tell them apart
  • Trace a bill through Congress to the president, including vetoes, overrides, and pocket vetoes
  • Name the five stages of public policy and show how all three branches act after a law passes
  • Answer GED-style questions using excerpts, tables, charts, and cartoons

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Answer it before you move on.

screens.title: Primaries, General Elections, and Terms
screens.html:
Most American elections have two rounds.

  • A primary election (or a caucus, a meeting of party members) chooses each party's candidate, called the nominee. In a closed primary, only voters registered with that party may vote. In an open primary, any registered voter may choose one party's ballot.
  • The general election is the final contest between the nominees. Federal general elections are held on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.
OfficeNumberTerm
U.S. Representative4352 years
U.S. Senator100 (2 per state)6 years; about one-third elected every 2 years
President14 years; elected no more than twice (22nd Amendment, 1951)

Elections held halfway through a president's term are called midterm elections.

check.prompt: Dana is registered as an independent, not with any party. Her state holds an open primary. What can she do on primary day?
options: Choose one party’s ballot and vote to pick that party’s nominee
Vote only in the general election, because primaries are for party members
Vote on every party’s ballot so she can help pick all of the nominees
Cast her vote for the winner of the election, not for a party nominee
why: That describes a closed primary, where only registered party members may vote. An open primary lets any registered voter take part.
In an open primary a voter picks one party’s ballot, not all of them.
Primaries choose each party’s nominee. The officeholder is chosen later, in the general election.
check.hint: Open primary vs. closed primary: who is allowed in?
check.explain: In an open primary, any registered voter may choose one party's ballot, so Dana can help pick that party's nominee. If the primary were closed, she could not vote in it because she is not registered with a party.

screens.title: The Electoral College
screens.html:
When you vote for president, you are really choosing a group of electors who promise to support your candidate. This system, the Electoral College, comes from Article II of the Constitution.

A state's electoral votes = its House members + 2 senators.
The District of Columbia gets 3 (23rd Amendment, 1961).
Total: 435 + 100 + 3 = 538. To win, a candidate needs a majority: 270.

House seats are divided among the states by population after every census (every 10 years), so a state's electoral votes can go up or down every 10 years. Because every state has two senators and at least one representative, the smallest number any state can have is 3.

example.prompt: A state has 14 members in the House. How many electoral votes does it have? A different state has 10 electoral votes. How many House members does it have?
steps: First state: House members + 2 senators = 14 + 2 = 16.
Second state: work backward. 10 − 2 senators = 8 House members.

check.prompt: A state has 12 members in the House of Representatives. How many electoral votes does it have?

mistakes.why: That is only the House members. Add 2 for the state’s two senators: 12 + 2.
Every state has two senators, not one. Add 2: 12 + 2 = 14.
The extra 3 electoral votes belong to the District of Columbia, not to each state. A state adds only its 2 senators.

check.hint: Use the formula: House members plus the number of senators every state has.

screens.title: Winner-Take-All and Results Tables
screens.html:
In 48 states and D.C., the candidate who wins the most votes in the state gets all of that state's electoral votes. This is called winner-take-all. (Maine and Nebraska can split their votes by district.)

When the GED gives you a results table, work in this order:

  1. Find the majority needed (more than half of the total electoral votes).
  2. Find the winner of each state.
  3. Add up electoral votes only for each candidate.
  4. Look at popular votes only if the question asks about them.

steps: Total 9 + 7 + 5 = 21; majority = 11.
State winners: Alpha, Lee; Beta, Moss; Gamma, Moss.
Electoral votes: Lee 9; Moss 7 + 5 = 12.
Popular votes: Lee 1,100,000; Moss 950,000.
example.answer: Moss wins with 12 electoral votes, even though Lee received 150,000 more popular votes.

check.prompt:
StateElectoral votesHalePrice
North12700,000520,000
South8410,000430,000
East6250,000260,000
West5190,000200,000

The country uses winner-take-all. How many electoral votes does Price win?

mistakes.why: You gave Price the votes of North, the state Hale won. Price won South, East, and West: 8 + 6 + 5.
That is the total of all four states. Price gets electoral votes only from the states Price won.
You added only South and East. Price also won West (200,000 > 190,000): 8 + 6 + 5 = 19.

check.hint: Find the winner of each row first. Then add only the electoral votes from the rows Price won.
check.explain: Price wins South (430,000 > 410,000), East (260,000 > 250,000), and West (200,000 > 190,000). Electoral votes: 8 + 6 + 5 = 19. Hale wins only North (12). Notice that Hale actually has more popular votes (1,550,000 to 1,410,000) but loses the electoral vote 12 to 19.

screens.title: When the Popular Vote and Electoral Vote Disagree
screens.html:
Winner-take-all means a big win in one state earns no more electoral votes than a narrow win. So a candidate can win the most votes nationwide and still lose the Electoral College. This is usually counted as having happened five times: 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016.

What if no candidate reaches 270? The 12th Amendment (1804) says the House of Representatives chooses the president from the top three candidates. Each state's House delegation casts one vote, so a large state and a small state count the same. The Senate chooses the vice president. The House last chose a president after the election of 1824.

Remember: The popular vote decides each state. The electoral vote decides the presidency.

check.prompt: Candidate Reyes wins three large states by huge margins. Candidate Owens wins seven smaller states by narrow margins and ends up with more electoral votes. Which statement best explains how Owens can win while receiving fewer popular votes?
options: Each state’s electoral votes go to its winner, however large or small the margin.
Electoral votes are divided among the candidates by their share of the national vote.
The House of Representatives chooses the winner whenever the popular vote is close.
Smaller states receive more electoral votes than larger states with more people.
why: That is not how nearly every state works. Under winner-take-all, the state winner gets all of its electoral votes; nothing is divided by national vote share.
The House chooses only when no candidate wins a majority of electoral votes, not when the popular vote is close.
Larger states have more electoral votes, because House seats follow population. Small states only get more votes per person.
check.hint: What does a candidate earn for winning a state by 1 vote compared with 1 million votes?
check.explain: Under winner-take-all, Reyes's extra votes in the states Reyes won so easily count for nothing extra, while Owens collects all the electoral votes in many states won narrowly. Total electoral votes, not total popular votes, decide the presidency.

screens.title: Political Parties
screens.html:
A political party is an organization that tries to win elections so it can control government. Parties:

  • nominate candidates for office (their most important job),
  • write a platform, a statement of goals (each goal is a plank),
  • inform voters and encourage them to vote, and
  • help organize government: leaders such as the Speaker of the House and the Senate majority leader are chosen through the parties.

Parties are not mentioned in the Constitution. In his Farewell Address (1796), George Washington warned against "the baneful effects of the spirit of party." (Baneful means harmful.) Even so, the first parties formed in the 1790s around Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson. The two major parties today are the Democratic Party and the Republican Party (founded 1854).

check.prompt: Which two are jobs of a political party? Select two answers.
options: Nominating candidates for public office
Writing a platform that states the party’s goals
Vetoing bills passed by Congress
Ruling on whether laws follow the Constitution
Writing regulations to carry out laws
why: Vetoing bills is a power of the president, not of a party.
Ruling on whether laws are constitutional is a job of the courts.
Writing regulations is done by executive branch agencies, not parties.
check.hint: Two of the choices belong to a party. The others belong to a branch of government.
check.explain: Parties nominate candidates and write platforms. The other three choices are official powers of a branch of government: the president vetoes, courts decide constitutionality, and agencies write regulations.

screens.title: Why Two Parties? The Role of Third Parties
screens.html:
The United States has a two-party system. Most elections give the seat to the one candidate with the most votes in a district, and most states give all of their electoral votes to one winner. A smaller party that finishes second or third everywhere can win nothing.

Third parties (any party other than the two major ones) still matter:

  • In 1992, independent candidate Ross Perot won about 19 percent of the popular vote but zero electoral votes.
  • The Populist Party of the 1890s called for voters to elect senators directly. The 17th Amendment (1913) later made that the law.

Third parties often raise ideas that a major party later adopts.

check.prompt: Based on this screen, which statement about third parties in the United States is best supported?
options: Their candidates rarely win, but their ideas are sometimes adopted by the major parties.
Their candidates are kept off the ballot by the Constitution, so they cannot win offices.
Their candidates win electoral votes in proportion to their share of the popular vote.
Their candidates have won most presidential elections held since the 1890s.
why: The Constitution does not mention parties at all and does not bar third-party candidates. They lose mainly because of one-winner districts.
Perot won about 19 percent of the vote and zero electoral votes, which shows votes are not shared out in proportion.
No third-party candidate has won the presidency in that period; the two major parties have won every time.
check.hint: Use the Perot and Populist examples on the screen.
check.explain: Third-party candidates rarely win because most elections have one winner per district and winner-take-all electoral votes. But their ideas can spread: the Populists' call for direct election of senators became the 17th Amendment. Perot's 19 percent and zero electoral votes disproves the idea of proportional electoral votes.

screens.title: Interest Groups and Their Methods
screens.html:
An interest group is an organization of people who share a goal and try to influence public policy, without running their own candidates. Types include business associations, labor unions, professional associations (doctors, teachers, nurses), and single-issue or public-interest groups.

Common methods:

  • Lobbying: contacting officials to persuade them
  • Testifying at committee hearings
  • Petitions, advertising, and public campaigns
  • Lawsuits: asking courts to rule on a law or policy
  • Campaign money through political action committees (PACs)

The First Amendment protects the right of the people "to petition the Government for a redress of grievances," which is the legal root of lobbying.

check.prompt:
Complete the sentences.

The Midstate Truckers Association meets privately with state senators to ask them to vote against a new fuel tax. This method is called {{0}}. Its political action committee also gives money to candidates who agree with it. When the tax passes anyway, the association files a case in court arguing the tax is illegal, which uses the {{1}} branch.

options: lobbying
nominating
filibustering
vetoing
why: Nominating means choosing a party’s candidate. The association is persuading officials, not choosing candidates.
A filibuster is long debate by a senator to block a vote. The association is not a senator.
Vetoing is the president’s (or a governor’s) power to reject a bill, not something an interest group can do.

options: judicial
legislative
executive
why: The legislature passed the tax. A lawsuit asks the courts, not lawmakers, to rule.
The executive branch carries out laws. A lawsuit is decided by the courts.

check.hint: What is the word for persuading officials? Which branch hears court cases?
check.explain: Meeting officials to persuade them is lobbying. Filing a case in court uses the judicial branch. Interest groups work through all three branches: lobbying Congress, commenting on agency rules, and suing in the courts.

screens.title: Party or Interest Group? The One-Question Test
screens.html:
Ask: Does the group nominate its own candidates to win control of government?
Yes = political party. No, it only tries to influence decisions = interest group.

Be careful with these look-alikes:

  • An interest group may endorse candidates (publicly back them) or give money through a PAC. That is still not nominating. The candidates were chosen by someone else.
  • A party may also lobby or hold rallies. What makes it a party is that it nominates candidates and seeks control of government.

example.prompt: The Riverbend Parents Network endorses two school board candidates and asks members to vote for them. It nominates no one. Party or interest group?
steps: Apply the test: does the network nominate its own candidates? No.
Endorsing someone else's candidate is support, not a nomination.

check.prompt: Which group is acting as a political party?
options: The Green Valley group holds a convention and chooses its own candidate for governor.
The Green Valley group endorses a candidate for governor and runs ads praising her.
The Green Valley group gives money through its PAC to two candidates for governor.
The Green Valley group testifies at a hearing on a bill the governor has proposed.
why: Endorsing and advertising back a candidate someone else nominated. Interest groups do this too; it is not nominating.
PAC donations support candidates but do not make the group their nominator. This is interest group activity.
Testifying at a hearing is a way to influence policy, a classic interest group method.
check.hint: Which group chooses its own candidate?
check.explain: Choosing its own candidate at a convention is nominating, the defining job of a political party. Endorsing, donating through a PAC, and testifying are all ways to influence government without running it, which interest groups do.

screens.title: How a Bill Moves Through Congress
screens.html:
1. Introduction. Only a member of Congress can introduce a bill. Anyone (a citizen, a group, the president) can suggest one. Bills for raising revenue (taxes) must start in the House (Article I, Section 7).
  2. Committee. A committee, often a subcommittee first, holds hearings and "marks up" (revises) the bill. Most bills die here.
  3. Floor vote. The full chamber debates and votes; passing takes a simple majority.
  4. The other chamber. The bill goes through the same steps in the other chamber. Both chambers must pass exactly the same text. A conference committee can work out differences.
  5. The president signs or vetoes the bill.

check.skill: How a bill becomes a law
check.prompt: A bill starts in the House and becomes law. Put the steps in order.
choices: The president signs the bill.
A House committee holds hearings and revises the bill.
A representative introduces the bill.
Both chambers pass one identical final version.
The full House debates and passes the bill.
check.why: The most common mistake is sending the bill to the president before both chambers have passed the identical version. The president can act only on the final, matching text.
check.hint: Committee comes before the floor vote, and both chambers must agree before the president acts.
check.explain: Order: (1) a representative introduces it, (2) a House committee holds hearings and revises it, (3) the full House passes it, (4) both chambers pass one identical version, (5) the president signs it.

screens.title: Filibuster and Cloture
screens.html:
The House limits debate; its Rules Committee sets how long each bill is debated. The Senate allows much longer debate. A senator (or group of senators) can keep talking or use the rules to block a vote. This is a filibuster.

To end debate, the Senate votes for cloture. On most bills, cloture takes three-fifths of the senators, which is 60 votes when all 100 seats are filled.

Do not mix up the numbers. 60 votes are needed to end debate. Passing the bill itself still takes a simple majority (51 of 100 when every senator votes).

check.prompt: All 100 Senate seats are filled. Senators opposed to a bill are filibustering. What is the smallest number of senators who must vote for cloture to end the debate?

mistakes.why: A simple majority (51) is enough to pass a bill. Ending a filibuster takes three-fifths: 3/5 × 100 = 60.
Two-thirds (67) is the vote needed to override a veto. Cloture takes three-fifths: 60.
Fifty is exactly half, not even a majority. Cloture takes three-fifths of 100, which is 60.

check.hint: Cloture takes three-fifths of the Senate.
check.explain: Cloture on most bills takes three-fifths of the Senate: 3/5 × 100 = 60 votes.

screens.title: The President's Four Outcomes
screens.html:
Article I, Section 7 gives the president four possible outcomes for a bill:

The president…Result
signs itIt becomes law.
vetoes it (returns it with objections)It dies unless two-thirds of both the House and the Senate vote to override.
does nothing for 10 days (Sundays excepted) while Congress is still meetingIt becomes law without a signature.
does nothing, and Congress adjourns before the 10 days are upIt dies. This is a pocket veto.

The deciding fact for the last two rows is whether Congress has adjourned.

check.prompt: Congress is meeting all summer. The president receives a bill on July 1 and neither signs it nor returns it. What happens after 10 days, not counting Sundays?
options: It becomes law without the president’s signature.
It dies, because the president did not sign it.
It goes back to Congress for a two-thirds vote.
It is sent to the Supreme Court for a decision.
why: A bill dies from inaction only if Congress has adjourned (a pocket veto). Congress is still meeting here.
A two-thirds vote is needed only to override a veto, and nothing was vetoed or returned.
The courts play no part in whether a bill becomes law. They can review a law only after it is passed.
check.explain: Article I, Section 7 says a bill not returned within ten days (Sundays excepted) "shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it," unless Congress has adjourned. Congress is still meeting, so the bill becomes law without a signature.

screens.title: Override Math
screens.html:
To override a veto, two-thirds of each chamber must vote yes. When every member votes:

  • House: 2/3 × 435 = 290 votes
  • Senate: 2/3 × 100 = 66.67, which rounds up to 67 votes (no one can cast part of a vote, and 66 is less than two-thirds)

Both chambers must reach two-thirds. If either one falls short, the veto stands.

example.prompt: The president vetoes a bill. Every member votes. House: 300 vote to override. Senate: 64 vote to override. Is the veto overridden?
steps: House: needs 290; got 300. The House succeeds.
Senate: needs 67; got 64. The Senate fails.
An override needs both chambers.
example.answer: No. The veto stands, and the bill does not become law.

check.prompt: All 435 members of the House vote on overriding a veto. What is the smallest number of "yes" votes the House needs?

mistakes.why: That is a simple majority of 435. An override needs two-thirds: 2/3 × 435 = 290.
2/3 × 435 is exactly 290, a whole number, so no rounding up is needed. 290 votes is two-thirds.
That is three-fifths of 435, the kind of fraction used for Senate cloture. A veto override takes two-thirds: 290.

check.explain: 2/3 × 435 = 870 ÷ 3 = 290. With 290 "yes" votes, the House reaches exactly two-thirds.

screens.title: Reading Article I, Section 7
screens.html:
The GED often quotes the Constitution and asks you to apply it. Old legal sentences pack several rules together. Find the turning words (if, but, unless) and split the text into cases.

Read this excerpt one sentence at a time:

"All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives; but the Senate may propose or concur with Amendments as on other Bills." (originate = begin; concur = agree)

"If any Bill shall not be returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him, the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it, unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law."

check.prompt: Click the part of Article I, Section 7 that describes a pocket veto.
spans: All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives;
but the Senate may propose or concur with Amendments as on other Bills.
If any Bill shall not be returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him,
the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it,
unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law.
check.why: The most tempting wrong click is "the Same shall be a Law," which describes a bill becoming law without a signature while Congress is still meeting. The pocket veto is the exception that follows "unless."
check.hint: Look for the turning word that introduces the exception.
check.explain: A pocket veto happens when Congress's adjournment prevents the president from returning the bill, "in which Case it shall not be a Law." The part before "unless" describes the opposite case: Congress is still meeting, so the unsigned bill becomes law.

screens.title: The Five Stages of Public Policy
screens.html:
Public policy is what government decides to do (or not do) about a public problem. It moves through five stages:

  1. Agenda setting: the problem gets the attention of leaders (complaints, news stories, petitions).
  2. Formulation: officials develop and compare possible solutions. No vote yet.
  3. Adoption: a law or decision is approved (a vote, a signature).
  4. Implementation: government agencies carry it out (hire, build, enforce).
  5. Evaluation: officials check whether it worked (reports, studies of results).

check.prompt: A town deals with a dangerous intersection. Drag each event into its policy stage.
choices: Parents pack a council meeting to complain about near-misses at the corner.
The town engineer compares a stop sign, a traffic light, and a roundabout.
The council votes to install a traffic light.
The public works department installs the light.
check.why: The most common mistake is putting the engineer’s comparison under adoption. Comparing options is formulation; adoption happens only when the council votes.
check.hint: Look for clue words: complain, compare, vote, install.
check.explain: Complaints put the problem on the agenda. Comparing options is formulation. The council's vote is adoption. Public works installing the light is implementation. A later report on accidents would be evaluation.

screens.title: The Branches in Action After a Law Passes
screens.html:
All three branches stay involved after a law is passed.

  • Executive: carries out the law. Federal agencies write detailed rules called regulations. Example: the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 created OSHA, which writes and enforces workplace safety rules.
  • Judicial: decides cases about the law and can rule that a law violates the Constitution (judicial review, from Marbury v. Madison, 1803).
  • Legislative: controls the money (the "power of the purse"), holds oversight hearings to check how the law is working, and can change the law. The Senate confirms the president's nominees for agency heads and federal judges.

check.prompt:
Complete the sentences.

After a new food-safety law passes, the Food and Drug Administration writes detailed inspection rules. This is the {{0}} branch at work. Later, a House committee calls the agency head to a hearing to ask why inspections are behind schedule. This is an example of {{1}}.

options: executive
legislative
judicial
why: Congress passed the law, but an agency writing rules to carry it out is part of the executive branch.
Courts decide cases; they do not write inspection rules.

options: oversight
judicial review
a filibuster
a pocket veto
why: Judicial review is a court ruling on whether a law is constitutional. A House hearing is Congress checking an agency.
A filibuster is a Senate tactic to block a vote, not a House hearing.
A pocket veto is the president letting a bill die when Congress adjourns.

check.hint: Who carries out laws? What do we call Congress checking on an agency?
check.explain: Agencies such as the FDA belong to the executive branch and write regulations to carry out laws. A congressional hearing that checks how an agency is doing its job is oversight, one way Congress checks the executive branch.

screens.title: Reading Election Data and Cartoons
screens.html:
GED questions on this topic often use a chart or a political cartoon.

Charts and tables: read the title, labels, and units. Then test each answer choice against the numbers. Watch for three traps: answers that reverse the data, answers that add a fact the chart does not show, and answers that predict or claim a cause the data cannot prove.

Cartoons: list the labels and symbols, notice exaggeration, and read the caption. The main point is what the details add up to, not any one detail.

A cartoon shows a tiny bill trying to climb a huge staircase labeled "Committee," "Floor Vote," "Other Chamber," and "President," with many crumpled bills at the bottom. Main point: passing a law is hard, and most bills fail along the way.

check.prompt:

Oakdale (a fictional city) began mailing every voter a ballot in 2020. Which conclusion is best supported by the table alone?
options: Turnout rose by 11 percentage points from 2019 to 2021.
Mailing ballots caused turnout to rise in 2021.
Turnout will keep rising in Oakdale’s 2023 election.
Turnout fell between 2017 and 2019, then recovered.
why: The rise came after the change, but the table alone cannot prove the mailed ballots caused it. Other factors could explain it.
A table of past results cannot prove what will happen in a future election.
This reverses the data: turnout rose from 22% to 24% between 2017 and 2019.
check.hint: Choose the answer you can prove with the numbers alone.
check.explain: From 2019 to 2021, turnout went from 24% to 35%: 35 − 24 = 11 percentage points. The tempting answer about mailed ballots claims a cause; the timing fits, but the table alone cannot rule out other reasons.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Elections: primaries or caucuses pick nominees (closed = party members only; open = any registered voter); the general election picks the winner. House 2-year terms, Senate 6, president 4 (two-term limit).
  • Electoral College: House + 2 per state; D.C. 3; total 538; win with 270. Winner-take-all in 48 states and D.C. No majority: the House picks, one vote per state.
  • Parties nominate candidates, write platforms, and organize government. Interest groups lobby, testify, petition, advertise, sue, and give through PACs, but do not nominate candidates.
  • Lawmaking: introduce → committee → floor → other chamber (identical text) → president. Revenue bills start in the House. Cloture = 60 senators.
  • President: sign = law; veto = dies unless 2/3 of both chambers override; 10 days with Congress meeting = law; Congress adjourned = pocket veto.
  • Policy: agenda setting → formulation → adoption → implementation → evaluation. Executive carries out laws; courts review them; Congress funds and oversees.

Next: the Practice set. Read every explanation, even on questions you get right.

stimuli.title: Document 1: The U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 7 (excerpt)
stimuli.html:
All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives; but the Senate may propose or concur with Amendments as on other Bills.

[The section goes on to say that every bill passed by both the House and the Senate must be presented to the president. The president must either sign the bill or return it, with written objections, to the chamber where it began. That chamber reconsiders the bill. If two thirds of that chamber vote to pass it again, the bill and the objections go to the other chamber for the same process]… and if approved by two thirds of that House, it shall become a Law…. If any Bill shall not be returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him, the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it, unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law.

originate = begin; concur = agree. Text in brackets summarizes part of the section in plain language; the rest is the Constitution's own wording.
stimuli.source: Constitution of the United States, Article I, Section 7 (1787)

stimuli.title: Document 2: George Washington's Farewell Address (excerpt)
stimuli.html:
Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally….

It serves always to distract the public councils and enfeeble the public administration. It agitates the community with ill-founded jealousies and false alarms, kindles the animosity of one part against another, foments occasionally riot and insurrection….

There is an opinion that parties in free countries are useful checks upon the administration of the government and serve to keep alive the spirit of liberty. This within certain limits is probably true…. But in those of the popular character, in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged.

baneful = harmful; enfeeble = weaken; animosity = hostility; foments = stirs up; "those of the popular character" = governments run by the people

stimuli.title: The Mill Road Flooding Problem
stimuli.html:
Riverside is a fictional town.

(1) For years, heavy rain flooded Mill Road, forcing the town to close it to traffic about six times a year. (2) In 2023, residents formed the Mill Road Neighbors Association. (3) Members collected 1,200 signatures on a petition, spoke at a town council meeting, and met with council members one by one. (4) The association did not endorse or run any candidates in the town election; its members said they cared only about fixing the road. (5) The association's president told the local newspaper, "Fixing this road is the most important job the council has."

(6) The council asked the town engineer to study three options: raising the road, building larger storm drains, or making no changes. (7) In 2024, the council voted 5–2 to spend $2.1 million on larger storm drains. (8) The town's public works department hired a contractor, and the drains were finished in 2025. (9) One year later, the public works department reported that Mill Road had been closed only once because of flooding.

stimuli.title: Political Cartoon (described)
stimuli.html: The cartoon shows a huge hedge maze labeled "CONGRESS." A small rolled-up paper with legs, labeled "BILL," walks in through the entrance. Signs inside the maze point in different directions: "SUBCOMMITTEE," "COMMITTEE," "RULES," "FLOOR VOTE," "OTHER CHAMBER," and "CONFERENCE." Far away, at the only exit, is a desk labeled "PRESIDENT." In a dead end near the entrance, a large pile of crumpled papers is labeled "BILLS THAT NEVER MADE IT." The tired little bill says, "Is it always this hard to become a law?"

stimuli.title: Document 3: Choosing the President (excerpts)
stimuli.html:
Article II, Section 1: Each State shall appoint, in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct, a Number of Electors, equal to the whole Number of Senators and Representatives to which the State may be entitled in the Congress: but no Senator or Representative, or Person holding an Office of Trust or Profit under the United States, shall be appointed an Elector.

Twelfth Amendment (1804): The person having the greatest number of votes for President, shall be the President, if such number be a majority of the whole number of Electors appointed; and if no person have such majority, then from the persons having the highest numbers not exceeding three on the list of those voted for as President, the House of Representatives shall choose immediately, by ballot, the President. But in choosing the President, the votes shall be taken by states, the representation from each state having one vote; a quorum for this purpose shall consist of a member or members from two-thirds of the states, and a majority of all the states shall be necessary to a choice.

appoint = choose; elector = a person who casts an official vote for president; "Office of Trust or Profit under the United States" = a federal government job; quorum = the smallest number of members who must be present to hold a vote
stimuli.source: Constitution of the United States, Article II, Section 1 (1787), and the Twelfth Amendment (1804)

stimuli.title: Document 4: James Madison, The Federalist No. 10 (excerpt)
stimuli.html:
By a faction, I understand a number of citizens, whether amounting to a majority or a minority of the whole, who are united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adverse to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community.

There are two methods of curing the mischiefs of faction: the one, by removing its causes; the other, by controlling its effects.

There are again two methods of removing the causes of faction: the one, by destroying the liberty which is essential to its existence; the other, by giving to every citizen the same opinions, the same passions, and the same interests.

It could never be more truly said than of the first remedy, that it was worse than the disease. Liberty is to faction what air is to fire, an aliment without which it instantly expires. But it could not be less folly to abolish liberty, which is essential to political life, because it nourishes faction, than it would be to wish the annihilation of air, which is essential to animal life, because it imparts to fire its destructive agency.

The second expedient is as impracticable as the first would be unwise…. The inference to which we are brought is, that the CAUSES of faction cannot be removed, and that relief is only to be sought in the means of controlling its EFFECTS.

faction = a group united by a shared interest, such as a party or an interest group; actuated = moved to act; adverse = opposed; aggregate = combined; mischiefs = harms; aliment = food; expedient = method; impracticable = not workable
stimuli.source: James Madison, The Federalist No. 10, published November 1787

stimuli.title: The Route 9 Crossing
stimuli.html:
Harlow County is a fictional county.

(1) In 2022, three children were hurt by cars while walking to Cedar Creek Elementary School along Route 9. (2) A group of parents formed Safe Steps for Kids. (3) The group collected 900 signatures and spoke at two county commission meetings. (4) That same year, the small Harlow County Forward Party nominated retired nurse Ana Bell as its candidate for county commissioner, and she campaigned on fixing Route 9. (5) Safe Steps for Kids did not nominate anyone; its leaders said they would work with whoever won.

(6) The county's transportation office studied three options: a traffic light, a crossing guard, or a lower speed limit. (7) In 2023, the commission voted 4–1 to install a traffic light and paint a marked crosswalk. (8) The transportation office hired a contractor, and the light began operating in March 2024. (9) In 2025, the transportation office reported that no children had been injured on that stretch of Route 9 since the light was installed.
