Each person carries a megaphone and a fat folder, and their name tags read "BANKERS' ASSOCIATION," "FARM BUREAU," "TEACHERS' UNION," "DRUG MAKERS," and "CLEAN WATER ALLIANCE." At the very end of the line, far outside the building, a woman in work clothes holds a small handwritten note. Her name tag reads "JUST A VOTER." She says, "I wonder if he'll ever get to me."

items.prompt: According to the excerpt, where must a bill for raising revenue (taxes) begin?
options: In the House of Representatives
In the Senate
In either chamber of Congress
In the office of the president
why: The Senate appears in the same sentence, but only as a body that "may propose or concur with Amendments." It can change a revenue bill, not start one.
The excerpt names one chamber, the House. "Either chamber" ignores the word "originate."
The president receives bills after Congress passes them. The excerpt says nothing about bills starting with the president.
items.hint: Look at the first sentence. What does "originate" mean?
items.explain:
The first sentence says, "All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives." Originate means begin, so tax bills must start in the House.

The most tempting wrong answer is the Senate, because it is mentioned in the same sentence. But the Senate may only "propose or concur with Amendments": it can change a revenue bill, not start one.

items.prompt: The president returns a bill to Congress with objections. Then two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate vote to pass the bill again. Based on the excerpt, what happens to the bill?
options: It becomes a law.
It goes to the Supreme Court for a final decision.
It goes back to the president for a second veto.
It must be sent to a committee and introduced again.
why: The excerpt never mentions the Supreme Court. Courts can review a law later, but they do not decide whether an overridden bill becomes law.
Nothing in the excerpt sends the bill back to the president. The override is Congress’s final answer to the veto.
The excerpt says that after two-thirds of both chambers approve it, "it shall become a Law." No new introduction is needed.
items.hint: Find the words "two thirds" in the excerpt and read to the end of that sentence.
items.explain:
The excerpt says that if two thirds of the first chamber vote to pass the bill again, it goes to the other chamber, "and if approved by two thirds of that House, it shall become a Law." This is a veto override, Congress's check on the president.

The most tempting wrong answer is a second veto, but the excerpt gives the president no further step once both chambers override.

items.skill: How a bill becomes a law
items.prompt: A bill begins in the House of Representatives and becomes a law. Drag each step into the correct order, from first to last.
choices: The Senate passes its own version of the bill.
A member of the House introduces the bill.
The president signs the bill.
A House committee holds hearings and revises the bill.
The two chambers settle their differences, and both pass one final version.
The full House debates and passes the bill.
items.why: The most common mistake is sending the bill to the president right after the Senate votes. The two versions differ, and the president can act only on a bill both chambers passed in exactly the same form.
items.hint: A bill must pass both chambers in exactly the same form before the president sees it.
items.explain:
1. A member of the House introduces the bill.
  2. A House committee holds hearings and revises it (most bills die at this step).
  3. The full House debates and passes it.
  4. The Senate passes its own version.
  5. The chambers settle their differences (for example, in a conference committee) and both pass the identical final version.
  6. The president signs it.

A common mistake is sending the bill to the president right after the Senate votes. The president can only act on a bill that both chambers have passed in exactly the same form.

items.prompt: After the 2020 census, a state has 7 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives. How many electoral votes does the state have?

mistakes.why: That counts only the House seats. Every state also gets 2 electoral votes for its senators: 7 + 2.
Every state has two senators, so add 2, not 1: 7 + 2 = 9.
The 3 extra electoral votes belong to the District of Columbia, not to each state. Add only the 2 senators.

items.hint: House seats plus the number of senators every state has.
items.explain:
Electoral votes = House seats + 2 senators = 7 + 2 = 9.

A common error is answering 7, which forgets the two electoral votes every state gets for its senators.

items.prompt: Which statement is supported by the table?
options: Grant received more popular votes, but Ellis received more electoral votes.
Ellis won North, the state with the most electoral votes in Norland.
Grant won a majority of the five states and most of the electoral votes.
No candidate won a majority of electoral votes, so the race had no winner.
why: Grant won North (1,300,000 to 900,000). You may have read the Ellis and Grant columns in reverse.
Grant won only one state, North. Ellis won the other four.
Ellis won 19 electoral votes, more than the 15 needed, so Ellis won outright.
items.hint: Find the winner of each state first, then add up the electoral votes. Then add up the popular votes separately.
items.explain:
Electoral votes: Grant wins North (1,300,000 > 900,000) for 10. Ellis wins South, East, West, and Central for 7 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 19.

Popular votes: Ellis: 900,000 + 520,000 + 410,000 + 330,000 + 260,000 = 2,420,000. Grant: 1,300,000 + 480,000 + 390,000 + 300,000 + 250,000 = 2,720,000.

So Grant has 300,000 more popular votes, but Ellis has more electoral votes (19 to 10). The tempting "no winner" choice forgets that 19 is more than the 15 needed.

items.prompt: How many electoral votes did Candidate Ellis receive?

mistakes.why: That is every electoral vote in Norland. Under winner-take-all, Ellis gets votes only from the states Ellis won.
That is Grant’s total from North. Ellis won the other four states: 7 + 5 + 4 + 3.
You left out one of Ellis’s states. Ellis won South, East, West, and Central: 7 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 19.

items.hint: Ellis gets a state's electoral votes only in states where Ellis has more votes than Grant.
items.explain:
Step 1: Find the states Ellis won. South (520,000 > 480,000), East (410,000 > 390,000), West (330,000 > 300,000), and Central (260,000 > 250,000). Grant won North.

Step 2: Add those states' electoral votes: 7 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 19.

A common error is answering 29 (all electoral votes) or trying to split each state's votes by percentage. In a winner-take-all system, the loser of a state gets none of its electoral votes.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the table and graph?
options: Each electoral vote in Wyoming represents fewer people than each one in California.
California has more electoral votes per person than Wyoming because it has more people.
Vermont and Wyoming have the same electoral votes because their populations are equal.
Texas has more House seats than California because Texas has more electoral votes.
why: This reverses the data. California’s bar is taller, so each of its electoral votes stands for more people, which means fewer electoral votes per person.
Both states have 3 electoral votes, but their populations differ (643,077 and 576,851). Each has 1 House seat + 2 senators.
The table shows Texas has fewer House seats (38) and fewer electoral votes (40) than California (52 and 54).
items.hint: Compare the heights of the bars. What does a shorter bar mean about each electoral vote?
items.explain:
The graph shows about 192,000 people per electoral vote in Wyoming (576,851 ÷ 3) and about 732,000 in California (39,538,223 ÷ 54). So each Wyoming electoral vote stands for fewer people. This happens because every state gets 2 electoral votes for its senators no matter how small it is.

The most tempting wrong answer reverses the data: "people per electoral vote" and "electoral votes per person" are opposites.

items.skill: Point of view in a primary source
items.prompt: Which statement best describes Washington's point of view on political parties in this excerpt?
options: Parties may check government, but in elected governments party spirit should not be encouraged.
Parties are necessary if a government elected by the people is going to work well and last.
Congress should pass an amendment banning political parties to protect the public councils.
Parties are dangerous in governments ruled by kings but helpful in governments run by the people.
why: This reverses his view. He warns that party spirit "enfeeble[s] the public administration," and says it is "not to be encouraged" in elected governments.
The excerpt warns against parties but never mentions Congress or an amendment. That is outside information.
This flips his point. He says party spirit is most to be avoided "in governments purely elective," that is, governments run by the people.
items.hint: Read the last paragraph closely. What does Washington grant, and what does the word "But" introduce?
items.explain:
Washington grants that parties may be "useful checks upon the administration of the government," saying this is "within certain limits… probably true." Then he turns with "But": "in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged." Earlier he warns that party spirit weakens government and turns one group against another.

The most tempting wrong answer says parties help governments run by the people, but that is the opposite of his final sentence.

items.prompt: Which two of the following are functions of political parties in the United States? Select two answers.
options: Nominating candidates to run for public office
Helping organize the leadership of each chamber of Congress
Signing bills into law
Deciding whether laws follow the Constitution
Counting the electoral votes in a joint meeting of Congress
why: Signing bills is a power of the president, an official of the executive branch, not of a party.
Deciding whether laws are constitutional is the job of the courts (judicial review).
Congress counts electoral votes as an official government duty. Parties do not count the votes.
items.hint: Two of the choices are jobs that belong to a specific branch of government, not to a party.
items.explain:
Correct: Nominating candidates is a party's most important job. Parties also organize Congress: leaders such as the Speaker of the House and the Senate majority leader are chosen through the parties.

Incorrect: Signing bills is the president's power. Deciding whether laws are constitutional belongs to the courts. Counting electoral votes is done by Congress as a body in a joint meeting, as an official government duty.

items.prompt: What is the main point of the cartoon?
options: The lawmaking process has many steps, and many bills never become law.
Presidents veto most of the bills that Congress sends to their desks.
Congress should get rid of its committees so bills can pass more easily.
Bills move through Congress too quickly to be studied with any care.
why: The pile of failed bills is in a dead end near the entrance, not at the president’s desk. The cartoon blames the maze, not vetoes.
The cartoon shows that the process is hard, but it does not propose any solution, such as abolishing committees.
A maze suggests a slow, confusing journey, the opposite of "too quickly."
items.hint: Look at the maze, the many signs, and the pile of papers. What do these details suggest about a bill's journey?
items.explain:
The maze with many signs shows that a bill must pass through many steps, and the large pile of "BILLS THAT NEVER MADE IT" shows that many bills fail along the way. The bill's question, "Is it always this hard to become a law?", sums up the point.

The tempting veto answer misreads where the pile is: in a dead end near the entrance, long before the president's desk.

items.prompt:
Complete the paragraph about the Mill Road passage.

The petition and meetings with council members helped put the flooding problem on the council's {{0}}. When the town engineer studied three possible solutions, the policy was in the {{1}} stage. When the public works department hired a contractor and built the drains, the policy was in the {{2}} stage.

options: agenda
ballot
platform
veto list
why: A ballot lists candidates or questions for voters in an election. The petition was aimed at the council, not at voters.
A platform is a political party’s statement of goals. The council is a government body, not a party.
There is no "veto list." The residents wanted the council to pay attention to the problem, which is agenda setting.

options: formulation
implementation
evaluation
adoption
why: Implementation is carrying out a decision already made. When the engineer studied options, nothing had been decided yet.
Evaluation checks results after a policy is in place. No drains existed yet.
Adoption is the vote that approves one option. That came later, in sentence 7.

options: evaluation
implementation
agenda-setting
formulation
why: Evaluation came after the drains were built, when the department reported on results (sentence 9).
Agenda setting was at the start, when residents called attention to the problem.
Formulation was the engineer’s study of options, before the vote.

items.hint: The order is agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation, evaluation.
items.explain:
• Agenda: the petition and meetings got council members to pay attention to the problem. A platform belongs to a political party, and a ballot is used in elections.
  • Formulation: studying and comparing options (raise the road, build drains, change nothing) is developing possible solutions. Adoption came later, when the council voted 5–2.
  • Implementation: an agency carrying out the approved decision is implementation. Evaluation came after, when the department reported on results (sentence 9).

items.prompt: Congress passes a bill and presents it to the president on December 1. On December 4, Congress adjourns until the following year. The president never signs the bill and is unable to return it. Based on the excerpt, what happens to the bill?
options: It does not become a law, because Congress’s adjournment kept the president from returning it.
It becomes a law after ten days (Sundays excepted), even though the president never signed it.
It becomes a law as soon as Congress returns next year, because the president issued no veto.
It goes back to the House, where two-thirds of the members must vote to approve it a second time.
why: This uses only the first half of the last sentence. That rule applies while Congress is still meeting; here Congress adjourned, so the "unless" exception controls.
Nothing in the excerpt makes a bill law when Congress returns. Because Congress’s adjournment prevented its return, "it shall not be a Law."
A two-thirds vote is how Congress overrides a returned veto. The bill was never returned, so there is nothing to override.
items.hint: Read the last sentence of the excerpt all the way to the end. What does "unless" change?
items.explain:
The last sentence has two cases. Normally, a bill not returned within ten days (Sundays excepted) "shall be a Law." But the sentence continues: "unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law."

Here Congress adjourned on December 4, only three days after the bill was presented, so the president could not return it. The bill does not become a law. This is called a pocket veto.

The most tempting wrong answer, "becomes a law after ten days," applies only when Congress is still meeting. Because no objections were returned to Congress, there is no override vote to take; supporters would have to start over with a new bill.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the passage best shows that the Mill Road Neighbors Association acted as an interest group rather than as a political party?
options: Sentence 4, which says the group ran and endorsed no candidates and cared only about the road
Sentence 3, which says members collected signatures, spoke to the council, and met with members
Sentence 5, which quotes the group’s president calling the road the council’s most important job
Sentence 7, which says the council voted 5–2 to spend $2.1 million on larger storm drains
why: These are interest group methods, but parties also gather signatures and meet with officials. This sentence does not show what the group did not do, which is the real difference.
This is an opinion given to a newspaper. Anyone, party or interest group, can speak to the press.
This describes the council’s action, not the association’s.
items.hint: What is the one thing a political party does that an interest group does not do?
items.explain:
The key difference is that a political party nominates candidates to win control of government, while an interest group tries to influence decisions without running candidates. Sentence 4 says the association did not run or endorse candidates and focused on one issue, which is exactly what makes it an interest group.

The most tempting wrong answer is sentence 3, which describes lobbying and petitions. Those are interest group methods, but they do not rule out a party, because parties can do those things too.

items.prompt: Candidate Grant lost the election in Norland. How many more popular votes did Grant receive than Ellis in all five states combined?

mistakes.why: That is only Grant’s margin in North (1,300,000 − 900,000). Ellis won the other four states, which cuts into that lead. Add each candidate’s total first.
That is Grant’s total, not the difference. Subtract Ellis’s total, 2,420,000.
That is the difference in electoral votes (19 − 10). The question asks about popular votes.

items.hint: Add each candidate's votes across all five states, then subtract.
items.explain:
Grant: 1,300,000 + 480,000 + 390,000 + 300,000 + 250,000 = 2,720,000.
Ellis: 900,000 + 520,000 + 410,000 + 330,000 + 260,000 = 2,420,000.
Difference: 2,720,000 − 2,420,000 = 300,000.

Grant won the popular vote by 300,000 but lost the electoral vote 10 to 19, because Grant's huge 400,000-vote margin in North earned no extra electoral votes. Answering 400,000 uses only North.

items.prompt: The president vetoes a bill that began in the House. Every member of Congress votes on the override. In the House, 295 of 435 members vote to override. In the Senate, 66 of 100 senators vote to override. What happens?
options: The veto stands, because 66 senators is less than two-thirds of the Senate.
The bill becomes law, because both chambers voted by more than a majority.
The bill becomes law, because 66 senators rounds to two-thirds of the Senate.
The bill goes to a conference committee to settle the two chambers’ votes.
why: A majority is enough to pass a bill the first time, but an override takes two-thirds of each chamber.
Two-thirds of 100 is 66.67. Sixty-six is less than that, so the Senate needs 67. Round up, not down.
Conference committees settle differences in the text of a bill. An override vote either reaches two-thirds or fails.
items.hint: Find two-thirds of 435 and of 100. Can you cast part of a vote?
items.explain:
House: 2/3 × 435 = 290. 295 ≥ 290, so the House succeeds.
Senate: 2/3 × 100 = 66.67, so 67 votes are needed. 66 < 67, so the Senate fails.
An override needs two-thirds of both chambers, so the veto stands.

The most tempting wrong answer rounds 66.67 down to 66. A vote of 66 out of 100 is less than two-thirds, so it falls short.

items.prompt: According to Article II, Section 1, how is the number of electors for each state decided?
options: It equals the state’s senators plus its representatives in Congress.
It is set by the House of Representatives after each presidential election.
It is three electors for every state, no matter how many people live there.
It equals the number of state legislators who are serving in the state.
why: The House chooses the president only when no one has a majority. The excerpt ties the number of electors to Congress seats, not to a House decision.
Three is only the smallest possible number (1 representative + 2 senators). Larger states have more representatives and so more electors.
The state legislature decides how electors are chosen ("in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct"), not how many there are.
items.hint: Find the word "equal" in the first sentence.
items.explain:
The excerpt says each state appoints "a Number of Electors, equal to the whole Number of Senators and Representatives to which the State may be entitled in the Congress." So electors = representatives + 2 senators.

The tempting answer about state legislators confuses two ideas in the sentence: the legislature decides the manner of choosing electors, but Congress seats set the number.

items.prompt: Based on Article II, Section 1, which person may not be appointed an elector?
options: A sitting member of the U.S. Senate
A member of the state legislature
A voter who belongs to a political party
A former governor of the state
why: The excerpt bars people who hold a federal office ("under the United States"). A state legislator holds a state office, so the excerpt does not bar them.
The excerpt says nothing about party membership. Electors are usually loyal party members.
A former governor holds no office now, and a governorship is a state office, not "under the United States."
items.hint: Read the part of the first sentence that begins with "but no Senator."
items.explain:
The excerpt says "no Senator or Representative, or Person holding an Office of Trust or Profit under the United States, shall be appointed an Elector." A sitting U.S. senator is named directly.

The tempting wrong answer is the state legislator, but the ban covers members of Congress and federal officeholders only.

items.skill: How a bill becomes a law
items.prompt: A bill about national park rules begins in the Senate. The president vetoes it, and Congress overrides the veto. Drag each step into the correct order, from first to last.
choices: The House passes the identical bill.
Two-thirds of each chamber vote to pass the bill again, and it becomes law.
A senator introduces the bill.
The president vetoes the bill and returns it to the Senate with objections.
The full Senate debates and passes the bill.
A Senate committee holds hearings and marks up the bill.
items.why: The most common mistake is placing the override vote before the veto, or having the president act before the House passes the identical bill. The president sees the bill only after both chambers agree, and Congress overrides only after a veto is returned.
items.hint: Committee comes before the floor vote. The veto must come before the override.
items.explain:
1. A senator introduces the bill.
  2. A Senate committee holds hearings and marks it up.
  3. The full Senate passes it.
  4. The House passes the identical bill.
  5. The president vetoes it and returns it to the Senate, where it began.
  6. Two-thirds of each chamber vote to pass it again, and it becomes law.

A bill can begin in the Senate because it is not a revenue (tax) bill. The vetoed bill goes back to the chamber where it started.

items.prompt: A state has 16 electoral votes. How many members does it have in the U.S. House of Representatives?

mistakes.why: You added 2 instead of subtracting. The 16 electoral votes already include the 2 senators: 16 − 2.
Every state has two senators. Subtract 2, not 1: 16 − 2 = 14.
You subtracted 3, the number of electoral votes for the District of Columbia. A state subtracts only its 2 senators.

items.hint: Electoral votes = House members + 2. Work backward.
items.explain:
Electoral votes = House members + 2, so House members = electoral votes − 2 = 16 − 2 = 14.

The most common error is 18, which adds the senators again instead of removing them.

items.prompt: Which statement is supported by the table?
options: Ortiz won the most electoral votes but fell short of a majority.
Brandt won both the most electoral votes and the most popular votes.
Kim won no states, so Kim did not receive any electoral votes.
Ortiz won a majority of electoral votes and became the leader.
why: Brandt won the most popular votes (2,540,000) but only 14 electoral votes, fewer than Ortiz’s 18.
Kim won Ridge (450,000 is the highest number in that row), which gave Kim 8 electoral votes.
Ortiz has 18 electoral votes, short of the 21 needed. The national assembly must choose.
items.hint: With three candidates, the state winner has the highest number in the row, not necessarily more than half.
items.explain:
State winners: Harbor, Ortiz (12); Plains, Brandt (9); Ridge, Kim (8); Valley, Ortiz (6); Coast, Brandt (5).
Electoral votes: Ortiz 12 + 6 = 18; Brandt 9 + 5 = 14; Kim 8. Total 40.

No one reaches 21, so Ortiz leads but falls short of a majority. The tempting "Kim won no states" choice misses Ridge, where Kim had the most votes of the three candidates.

items.prompt: How many electoral votes did Ortiz receive?

mistakes.why: That counts only Harbor. Ortiz also won Valley (280,000 is the most in that row): 12 + 6.
That is Brandt’s total (Plains 9 + Coast 5). Ortiz won Harbor and Valley.
You gave Ortiz Plains too, but Brandt won Plains (650,000 > 610,000). Ortiz won only Harbor and Valley: 12 + 6.

items.hint: Find the highest number in each row. Add only the electoral votes from the rows Ortiz won.
items.explain:
Ortiz has the most votes in Harbor (1,050,000) and Valley (280,000). Electoral votes: 12 + 6 = 18.

A common error is giving Ortiz Plains, where Ortiz was close but finished second to Brandt.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: Of the six states shown, Texas gained the most electoral votes after the 2020 census.
Every state shown gained electoral votes after the 2020 census because of new House seats.
Florida and New York had the same number of electoral votes before and after the 2020 census.
The total number of electoral votes in the country rose after the 2020 census was counted.
why: Only Texas and Florida gained. California, New York, Pennsylvania, and Ohio each lost one electoral vote.
They were tied at 29 for 2012–2020, but after 2020 Florida has 30 and New York has 28.
The House stays at 435 seats, so the total stays at 538. Seats shift between states; the graph does not show a national increase.
items.hint: Compare the two bars for each state. Which state's second bar is highest above its first bar?
items.explain:
Texas went from 38 to 40 electoral votes, a gain of 2. Florida gained 1 (29 to 30). California, New York, Pennsylvania, and Ohio each lost 1. So Texas gained the most.

The tempting Florida/New York answer is true only for the first period. After the 2020 census they no longer match (30 and 28).

items.skill: Point of view in a primary source
items.prompt: Which statement best describes Madison's point of view on factions in this excerpt?
options: Factions cannot be removed without destroying liberty, so their effects should be controlled.
Factions should be removed by giving every citizen the same opinions, passions, and interests.
Factions are harmless because they serve the permanent and aggregate interests of the community.
Liberty should be limited in order to end factions, since factions threaten the whole community.
why: Madison lists this method only to reject it: he calls it "as impracticable as the first would be unwise."
This reverses his definition. He says factions are "adverse to" the rights of others and to "the permanent and aggregate interests of the community."
He says destroying liberty to end factions would be "worse than the disease," like destroying air to stop fire.
items.hint: Read the last sentence of the excerpt. What does Madison say can and cannot be done?
items.explain:
Madison names two ways to remove the causes of faction (destroying liberty, or making everyone think alike) and rejects both: the first is "worse than the disease" and the second is "impracticable." He concludes "that the CAUSES of faction cannot be removed, and that relief is only to be sought in the means of controlling its EFFECTS."

The tempting answer about limiting liberty uses his words but reverses his judgment; he compares that remedy to wishing away air to stop fire.

items.prompt: Which two are methods interest groups commonly use to influence public policy? Select two answers.
options: Testifying before a congressional committee about a bill
Filing a lawsuit that challenges a government regulation
Nominating its own candidate for the U.S. Senate
Casting votes on bills on the floor of the House
Vetoing a bill passed by the state legislature
why: Nominating candidates is what makes a group a political party. Interest groups influence policy without running their own candidates.
Only members of Congress vote on bills on the House floor. Interest groups try to persuade those members.
Vetoing is a power of the president or a governor, not of a private group.
items.hint: Two choices are official powers of government officials, and one is the job of a party.
items.explain:
Correct: Interest groups testify at hearings and file lawsuits. They also lobby, petition, advertise, and give money through PACs.

Incorrect: Nominating candidates is the defining job of a party. Voting on bills belongs to members of Congress, and vetoing belongs to the president or a governor.

items.prompt: What is the main point of the cartoon?
options: Organized interest groups can reach lawmakers more easily than individual voters can.
Lawmakers refuse to meet with any group that does not give money to their campaigns.
Interest groups should be banned because they keep lawmakers from doing their jobs.
Voters have more influence than interest groups because voters decide who is elected.
why: The cartoon shows the voter waiting at the back of the line, not being turned away, and it never mentions campaign money.
The cartoon points out a problem, but it does not call for banning interest groups; the groups even include teachers and clean-water advocates.
This reverses the cartoon. The voter is far outside the building, wondering if she will ever be heard.
items.hint: Compare the people at the front of the line with the person at the end. What do the megaphones and folders suggest?
items.explain:
The long line of well-organized groups with megaphones and fat folders, compared with the lone voter at the very end holding a small note, shows that organized interests have easier access to lawmakers. Her caption, "I wonder if he'll ever get to me," states the point. The "OPEN DOOR POLICY" sign adds irony: the door is open, but the groups fill it.

The tempting answer about campaign money adds a detail the cartoon does not show.

items.prompt:
Complete the paragraph about the Route 9 passage.

When the county commission voted 4–1 for a traffic light and crosswalk (sentence 7), the policy reached the {{0}} stage. When the transportation office hired a contractor and turned on the light (sentence 8), the policy was in the {{1}} stage. The 2025 report on injuries (sentence 9) is an example of {{2}}.

options: adoption
formulation
implementation
agenda-setting
why: Formulation was the study of three options in sentence 6. The vote chose one option, which is adoption.
Implementation is carrying out the decision. The vote made the decision; the building came later.
Agenda setting was the injuries and petition that drew attention to the problem (sentences 1–3).

options: implementation
evaluation
adoption
formulation
why: Evaluation checks results after the policy is in place. Here the light is just being built and turned on.
Adoption was the commission’s vote in sentence 7. Building the light carries that decision out.
Formulation means developing options. The option was already chosen.

options: evaluation
implementation
adoption
agenda setting
why: Implementation was installing the light. A report on results afterward is a different stage.
Adoption was the vote. A report on whether the light worked comes at the end.
The report looks back at results; it is not drawing first attention to a new problem.

items.hint: Clue words: voted = adoption; hired and built = implementation; reported results = evaluation.
items.explain:
• Adoption: the commission's vote approved one option.
  • Implementation: the transportation office, an executive agency, hired a contractor and turned on the light.
  • Evaluation: the 2025 report checked whether the policy worked.

The order of all five stages: agenda setting (sentences 1–3), formulation (sentence 6), adoption (7), implementation (8), evaluation (9).

items.prompt: In a fictional future election, no presidential candidate wins a majority of electoral votes. The House votes under the Twelfth Amendment. The delegations of 24 states vote for Adair, 20 for Bishop, and 6 for Cole. All 50 states are present. Based on the excerpt, what is the result of this vote?
options: No one is chosen yet, because a majority of all the states, 26, is necessary.
Adair is chosen, because Adair won more state delegations than anyone else.
Adair and Bishop go to the Senate, which then chooses between the top two.
The candidate with the most electoral votes from the states becomes president.
why: Winning the most states is a plurality, not a majority. The excerpt says "a majority of all the states shall be necessary to a choice": 26 of 50.
Under the Twelfth Amendment the House chooses the president. The excerpt gives the Senate no role in choosing the president.
The House vote happens because no one won an electoral majority. The excerpt replaces the electoral count with a vote by state delegations.
items.hint: How many states make a majority of 50? Did anyone reach it?
items.explain:
The Twelfth Amendment says that in the House "the votes shall be taken by states, the representation from each state having one vote," and "a majority of all the states shall be necessary to a choice." A majority of 50 states is 26. Adair has 24, so no one is chosen yet, and the House must keep voting.

The most tempting wrong answer chooses Adair for winning the most states, but the excerpt requires a majority, not just the most.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the passage best shows that the Harlow County Forward Party is a political party rather than an interest group?
options: Sentence 4, which says the Forward Party nominated Ana Bell as its candidate for commissioner
Sentence 3, which says a group collected 900 signatures and spoke at two commission meetings
Sentence 5, which says Safe Steps for Kids nominated no one and would work with whoever won
Sentence 7, which says the county commission voted 4–1 to install a light and a crosswalk
why: Sentence 3 describes Safe Steps for Kids using petitions and testimony, which are interest group methods. It is not about the Forward Party.
Sentence 5 shows that Safe Steps for Kids is not a party. It says nothing about the Forward Party.
Sentence 7 describes an action by the county government, not by the Forward Party.
items.hint: What does a party do that an interest group does not? Which sentence is about the Forward Party?
items.explain:
The defining job of a political party is nominating candidates to win control of government. Sentence 4 says the Forward Party "nominated retired nurse Ana Bell as its candidate for county commissioner," which makes it a party.

The tempting wrong answer is sentence 5, which uses the same test but applies it to a different group: it proves Safe Steps for Kids is an interest group.

items.prompt: Brandt received the most popular votes in Calloway but did not lead in electoral votes. How many more popular votes did Brandt receive than Ortiz in all five states combined?

mistakes.why: That is only the margin in Harbor (1,050,000 − 980,000), where Ortiz led. Add each candidate’s total across all five states first.
That is Brandt’s lead over Kim (2,540,000 − 1,510,000). The question compares Brandt with Ortiz.
That is the difference in electoral votes between Ortiz (18) and Brandt (14). The question asks about popular votes.

items.hint: Add the Brandt column and the Ortiz column separately, then subtract.
items.explain:
Brandt: 980,000 + 650,000 + 420,000 + 260,000 + 230,000 = 2,540,000.
Ortiz: 1,050,000 + 610,000 + 300,000 + 280,000 + 190,000 = 2,430,000.
Difference: 2,540,000 − 2,430,000 = 110,000.

Brandt leads the popular vote by 110,000 but trails Ortiz in electoral votes, 14 to 18. A common error is comparing Brandt with Kim instead of Ortiz.

items.prompt: The president vetoes a bill that began in the Senate. Every member of Congress votes on the override. In the Senate, 70 of 100 senators vote to override. In the House, 285 of 435 members vote to override. What happens?
options: The veto stands, because 285 is less than the 290 votes the House needs.
The bill becomes law, because the Senate passed it by more than two-thirds.
The bill becomes law, because 285 is more than half of the House’s 435 seats.
The veto stands, because a Senate bill can be overridden only by the Senate.
why: The Senate did reach two-thirds (70 ≥ 67), but an override needs two-thirds of both chambers.
More than half is a majority, which is enough to pass a bill the first time. An override needs two-thirds: 290.
Article I, Section 7 sends a vetoed bill to both chambers. Each chamber must reach two-thirds, no matter where the bill began.
items.hint: Check two-thirds in each chamber separately. Both must succeed.
items.explain:
Senate: 2/3 × 100 = 66.67, so 67 needed. 70 ≥ 67, so the Senate succeeds.
House: 2/3 × 435 = 290. 285 < 290, so the House fails.
An override needs both chambers, so the veto stands.

The most tempting wrong answer stops after the Senate succeeds. Like a door with two locks, both chambers must reach two-thirds.

stimuli.title: The U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 7 (excerpt)
stimuli.html:
Every Bill which shall have passed the House of Representatives and the Senate, shall, before it become a Law, be presented to the President of the United States; If he approve he shall sign it, but if not he shall return it, with his Objections to that House in which it shall have originated…. If any Bill shall not be returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him, the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it, unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law.

originated = began; adjournment = the end of a period of meetings
stimuli.source: Constitution of the United States, Article I, Section 7 (1787)

stimuli.html:
[After the president returns a bill with objections, the chamber where it began reconsiders it.] If after such Reconsideration two thirds of that House shall agree to pass the Bill, it shall be sent, together with the Objections, to the other House, by which it shall likewise be reconsidered, and if approved by two thirds of that House, it shall become a Law. But in all such Cases the Votes of both Houses shall be determined by Yeas and Nays, and the Names of the Persons voting for and against the Bill shall be entered on the Journal of each House respectively.

House = here, either chamber of Congress; yeas and nays = yes and no votes; journal = the official written record of a chamber

items.prompt: Why does every state have at least 3 electoral votes, no matter how small its population?
options: Every state has two senators and at least one member of the House.
The 23rd Amendment gives each state three electors as a starting point.
Small states get extra electors to balance the winner-take-all rule.
The census assigns every state three House seats before counting people.
why: The 23rd Amendment gave 3 electoral votes to the District of Columbia, not to every state.
No rule adds extra electors to small states. The minimum of 3 comes from the 2 Senate seats every state has plus at least 1 House seat.
Every state is guaranteed only one House seat. The other two electoral votes come from its senators.
items.explain: A state's electoral votes = its House members + 2 senators. Every state has 2 senators and at least 1 representative, so the smallest possible total is 1 + 2 = 3. The tempting 23rd Amendment answer confuses the states with the District of Columbia.

items.prompt: How many electoral votes did Patel receive?

mistakes.why: That is Quinn’s total (Hill only). Patel won Lake, Bay, and Mesa: 13 + 5 + 4.
You left out Mesa. Patel also won Mesa (170,000 > 160,000): 13 + 5 + 4 = 22.
That is every electoral vote in Dunmore. Patel gets votes only from the states Patel won.

items.explain: Patel wins Lake (820,000 > 790,000), Bay (230,000 > 215,000), and Mesa (170,000 > 160,000). Quinn wins Hill. Patel's electoral votes: 13 + 5 + 4 = 22.

items.prompt: The Rural Health Alliance runs TV ads urging Congress to fund rural clinics, endorses candidates who agree with it, and gives money through its PAC. It has never nominated a candidate. Which statement correctly classifies the Alliance?
options: It is an interest group, because it works to influence policy but nominates no candidates.
It is a political party, because it endorses candidates and gives them campaign money.
It is a political party, because it tries to change what Congress does about health care.
It is an interest group, because the law does not allow it to give candidates any money.
why: Endorsing and donating support candidates someone else nominated. Only nominating its own candidates would make it a party.
Trying to change what Congress does is exactly what interest groups do. Influencing policy is not the same as running for office.
The label is right but the reason is wrong: the passage says it gives money through its PAC, which is legal.
items.explain: The test is whether the group nominates its own candidates to win control of government. The Alliance has never nominated anyone; ads, endorsements, and PAC money are all ways to influence policy. So it is an interest group. The tempting "party" answer treats endorsing and donating as if they were nominating.

items.prompt:
Complete the sentences.

A group of senators is filibustering a bill. With all 100 seats filled, ending the debate takes at least {{0}} votes. Later, the president vetoes a different bill. Congress can still make it a law if {{1}} vote to override.

why: Fifty-one is a simple majority, enough to pass a bill but not to end a filibuster. Cloture takes three-fifths: 60.
Sixty-seven is two-thirds of the Senate, the number for a veto override, not for cloture.
Fifty is exactly half, not even a majority. Cloture takes three-fifths of 100: 60.

options: two-thirds of both the House and the Senate
a majority of both the House and the Senate
two-thirds of the Senate alone
three-fifths of both the House and the Senate
why: A majority passes a bill the first time. Overriding a veto takes two-thirds.
The House must also vote by two-thirds. An override needs both chambers.
Three-fifths is the fraction for Senate cloture. A veto override takes two-thirds.

items.explain: Cloture on most bills takes three-fifths of the Senate: 3/5 × 100 = 60. A veto override takes two-thirds of both the House and the Senate. Mixing up these two fractions is the most common error.

items.prompt: Congress is meeting through the spring. On March 2, the president receives a bill and neither signs it nor returns it. Twelve days pass, not counting Sundays. Based on the excerpt, what is the status of the bill?
options: It is a law, because the president held it more than ten days while Congress was meeting.
It is not a law, because the president never signed it during the ten-day period allowed.
It is not a law, because the president’s silence counts as a pocket veto of the bill.
It is waiting for Congress, which must pass it again by two-thirds to make it a law.
why: The excerpt says an unreturned bill becomes law "as if he had signed it." A signature is not required when the president lets the time run out.
A pocket veto happens only when Congress’s adjournment prevents the return. Congress is still meeting here.
A two-thirds vote is how Congress responds to a veto that was returned with objections. Nothing was returned.
items.explain: The excerpt says that if a bill is "not returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted)," it "shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it," unless Congress's adjournment prevented its return. Congress is still meeting, so the exception does not apply. The bill is a law. The tempting pocket veto answer ignores that Congress has not adjourned.

items.prompt: The fictional city of Lakeport responds to teen unemployment. Drag each event into its policy stage.
choices: A newspaper series on rising teen unemployment leads the city council to discuss the problem.
City staff compare three ideas: a summer jobs program, tax credits for employers, and a job fair.
The parks department hires 200 teens for summer work crews.
An end-of-summer report counts how many teens finished the program and found later jobs.
The city workforce office places other teens in jobs at local businesses.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the end-of-summer report under implementation. Running the program is implementation; measuring its results afterward is evaluation.
items.explain:
• Agenda setting: news coverage draws the council's attention to the problem.
  • Formulation: staff compare possible solutions before any vote.
  • Implementation: the parks department and the workforce office carry out the program.
  • Evaluation: the end-of-summer report measures whether it worked.

items.prompt: Congress passes a new airline safety law. Which action is an example of the judicial branch at work?
options: A federal court hears a case claiming part of the law is unconstitutional.
The Federal Aviation Administration writes inspection rules for airlines.
A Senate committee holds a hearing on how the new rules are working.
The president nominates a new leader for the aviation safety agency.
why: The FAA is an executive agency. Writing rules to carry out a law is the executive branch at work.
A Senate hearing is congressional oversight, the legislative branch at work.
Nominating agency leaders is a power of the president, the head of the executive branch.
items.explain: Courts decide cases and can rule that a law violates the Constitution (judicial review), so the court case is the judicial branch. The FAA writing rules is executive, the Senate hearing is legislative oversight, and the nomination is executive. The tempting FAA answer confuses carrying out a law with judging it.

items.prompt: Quinn lost the election in Dunmore. Which single change would have made Quinn the winner?
options: Quinn winning Lake instead of Patel
Quinn winning Bay instead of Patel
Quinn winning Mesa instead of Patel
Quinn gaining 300,000 more votes in Hill
why: Quinn would have 7 + 5 = 12 and Patel 13 + 4 = 17. Patel would still have a majority.
Quinn would have 7 + 4 = 11 and Patel 13 + 5 = 18. Patel would still win.
Quinn already won Hill. Under winner-take-all, extra votes there add no electoral votes; Quinn would still have 7.
items.explain:
Now: Patel 13 + 5 + 4 = 22; Quinn 7. Majority = 15.

  • Quinn wins Lake: Quinn 7 + 13 = 20, Patel 5 + 4 = 9. Quinn wins.
  • Quinn wins Bay: Quinn 12, Patel 17. Patel still wins.
  • Quinn wins Mesa: Quinn 11, Patel 18. Patel still wins.
  • More votes in Hill: Quinn stays at 7.

The tempting Hill answer ignores winner-take-all: Quinn already won Hill, so a bigger margin there changes nothing. Quinn actually had more popular votes (1,705,000 to 1,480,000) because of Hill.

items.prompt: In a presidential election, no candidate wins a majority of the electoral votes. Under the Twelfth Amendment, how is the president chosen?
options: The House chooses, and each state’s delegation casts one vote.
The Senate chooses, and each senator casts one vote for president.
The House chooses, and each representative casts one vote for president.
The candidate with the most popular votes nationwide becomes president.
why: The Senate chooses the vice president in this case. The House chooses the president.
The House votes by state, not by member: each state delegation casts a single vote.
When no one has an electoral majority, the Constitution sends the choice to the House, not to the popular vote.
items.explain: The Twelfth Amendment (1804) says the House of Representatives chooses from the top three candidates, with each state delegation casting one vote; a majority of the states is needed. The Senate chooses the vice president. The tempting answer gives every representative a vote, but the House votes by state.

items.prompt: How many more electoral votes did Vance receive than Wu?

mistakes.why: That is Vance’s total. Subtract Wu’s 9 electoral votes: 22 − 9.
You gave Vance only North (12) and Wu only South (9). Vance also won East, West, and Central: 22 − 9 = 13.
That is Wu’s lead in popular votes. The question asks about electoral votes.

items.explain:
Vance wins North (700,000 > 690,000), East, West, and Central: 12 + 5 + 3 + 2 = 22. Wu wins South: 9.
Difference: 22 − 9 = 13.

items.prompt: The Prairie Freedom Party holds a statewide primary to choose its candidate for governor and writes a platform calling for lower property taxes. It also lobbies the legislature on a tax bill. Which statement correctly classifies it?
options: It is a political party, because it nominates its own candidates to win control of government.
It is an interest group, because it lobbies the state legislature about a property tax bill.
It is an interest group, because it focuses mainly on one issue, lowering property taxes.
It is a political party, because any group that lobbies lawmakers is treated as a party.
why: Lobbying is something both parties and interest groups can do. What settles it is that the group nominates its own candidate.
Focusing on one issue does not decide the question. A group that nominates candidates for office is a party, even a single-issue party.
Lobbying does not make a group a party; most lobbying is done by interest groups.
items.explain: The group holds a primary to choose its own candidate for governor and writes a platform. Nominating candidates to win control of government is the defining job of a political party. Its lobbying does not change that, because parties can lobby too. The tempting interest group answer focuses on the lobbying and misses the nomination.

items.prompt:
Complete the sentences.

A bill that would raise income taxes must begin in the {{0}}. If the president does not sign a bill and Congress adjourns before the ten days are up, the bill {{1}}.

options: House of Representatives
Senate
either chamber of Congress
why: Article I, Section 7 says revenue bills "shall originate in the House." The Senate may only propose or agree to amendments.
Most bills may start in either chamber, but revenue bills are the exception: Article I, Section 7 requires them to start in the House.

options: dies in a pocket veto
becomes law without a signature
returns to Congress for an override vote
goes to the Supreme Court for review
why: A bill becomes law without a signature only while Congress is still meeting. Here Congress adjourned.
Nothing was returned, so there is no veto to override. A pocket veto cannot be overridden.
Courts do not decide whether a bill becomes law. The Constitution settles this case: "it shall not be a Law."

items.explain: Revenue (tax) bills must start in the House of Representatives. An unsigned bill dies if Congress adjourns before the ten days are up and the president cannot return it: a pocket veto. If Congress were still meeting, the same bill would become law without a signature.

items.prompt: A House leader proposes that the override vote on a vetoed bill be taken by a quick unrecorded voice vote, so no one's name is attached to it. Based on the excerpt, is this allowed?
options: No, because the votes must be by yeas and nays, with each member’s name recorded.
Yes, because each chamber may decide for itself how to vote on overriding a veto.
Yes, as long as two-thirds of the members present agree by voice that it passes.
No, because override votes must take place in a joint meeting of both chambers.
why: The excerpt sets the rule for "all such Cases," so neither chamber may choose a different method for an override.
Reaching two-thirds is required, but so is recording it: "the Names of the Persons voting for and against the Bill shall be entered on the Journal."
The excerpt has each chamber vote separately ("the other House… shall likewise" reconsider it). It does not call for a joint meeting.
items.explain: The excerpt says, "in all such Cases the Votes of both Houses shall be determined by Yeas and Nays, and the Names of the Persons voting for and against the Bill shall be entered on the Journal of each House." An unrecorded voice vote breaks that rule, so it is not allowed. The tempting two-thirds-by-voice answer meets the vote count but ignores the recording requirement.

items.prompt: A fictional state responds to a drought. Drag each event into its policy stage.
choices: Farmers testify to lawmakers that their wells are running dry.
The state water board drafts three plans: rationing, higher water prices, or a new reservoir.
The water board votes to approve a rationing plan.
The governor signs an emergency water bill passed by the legislature.
The water utility sends inspectors and fines households that break the rationing rules.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the governor’s signature under implementation. Signing a bill approves the policy, which is adoption; inspecting and fining is carrying it out.
items.explain:
• Agenda setting: farmers' testimony brings the problem to lawmakers' attention.
  • Formulation: drafting and comparing three plans.
  • Adoption: the board's vote and the governor's signature approve the policy.
  • Implementation: the utility's inspectors and fines carry it out.

items.prompt: Which action is an example of the legislative branch checking the executive branch?
options: The Senate votes to reject the president’s choice to lead a federal agency.
A federal agency writes new rules to carry out a law passed by Congress.
A federal court rules that an agency’s new rule goes beyond the law.
The president directs an agency to speed up its work on a new program.
why: Writing rules to carry out a law is the executive branch doing its own job, not a check on it.
This is a check on the executive branch, but by the judicial branch, not the legislative branch.
The president directing an agency is the executive branch managing itself.
items.explain: The Senate confirms (or rejects) the president's nominees for agency heads and federal judges. Rejecting a nominee is the legislative branch checking the executive. The tempting court ruling is also a check, but it comes from the judicial branch.

items.prompt: Wu received more popular votes than Vance but lost the election in Kestrel. Which detail from the table best explains why?
options: Wu won South by 340,000 votes, but that huge margin still earned only South’s 9 votes.
Wu came within 10,000 votes of Vance in North, the state with the most electoral votes.
Vance won Central by only 5,000 votes, the smallest margin of any state in the table.
Vance received 1,585,000 popular votes in all, which was more than half of all votes cast.
why: This shows Wu nearly won North, but losing narrowly still gives Vance all 12 votes. It describes a close loss; it does not explain why Wu had more popular votes yet lost.
This is true, but Central has only 2 electoral votes. It does not explain the gap between Wu’s popular and electoral totals.
This is false. Vance had 1,585,000 and Wu 1,880,000, so Vance had less than half of the 3,465,000 votes cast.
items.explain: Wu's popular vote lead (1,880,000 − 1,585,000 = 295,000) comes almost entirely from South, which Wu won by 720,000 − 380,000 = 340,000. Under winner-take-all, that huge margin earned only South's 9 electoral votes, while Vance's narrow wins in North, East, West, and Central earned 22. The tempting North answer describes a close race but does not explain the split between the popular and electoral votes.

vocab.def: An election in which voters choose a party's candidate for an office.
vocab.example: In a closed primary, only voters registered with that party may vote.

vocab.def: The final election in which voters choose among the nominees to fill an office.
vocab.example: Federal general elections are held on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.

vocab.def: The group of electors, chosen in each state and the District of Columbia, who cast the official votes for president and vice president.
vocab.example: There are 538 electors; a candidate needs 270 to win.

vocab.def: A person chosen to cast one of a state's electoral votes for president.
vocab.example: A state with 9 House members has 11 electors.

vocab.def: The votes cast directly by citizens in an election.
vocab.example: A candidate can win the national popular vote and still lose the Electoral College.

vocab.def: A system in which the candidate with the most votes in a state receives all of that state's electoral votes.
vocab.example: Winning a state by 1 vote earns the same electoral votes as winning it by 1 million.

vocab.def: An organization that nominates candidates and tries to win elections in order to control government.
vocab.example: The Democratic Party and the Republican Party are the two major parties today.

vocab.def: A party's written statement of its goals and positions. Each separate position is called a plank.
vocab.example: Parties adopt a platform at their national conventions.

vocab.def: Any political party other than the two major parties.
vocab.example: Third-party candidates rarely win, but their ideas are sometimes adopted by the major parties.

vocab.def: An organization of people with a shared goal who try to influence public policy without nominating their own candidates.
vocab.example: A teachers' association asks lawmakers to fund school repairs.

vocab.def: Contacting government officials to persuade them to support or oppose a policy.
vocab.example: A business group meets with senators about a trade bill.

vocab.def: An organization that raises money and gives it to candidates or campaigns, often for an interest group.
vocab.example: A labor union's PAC donates to candidates it supports.

vocab.def: The president's rejection of a bill passed by Congress. Congress can override it with a two-thirds vote in both chambers. A pocket veto happens when Congress adjourns and the unsigned bill cannot be returned.
vocab.example: The president returns the bill to Congress with a list of objections.

vocab.def: Extended debate in the Senate used to delay or block a vote. It can be ended by cloture, a vote of three-fifths of the Senate.
vocab.example: Ending a filibuster on most bills takes 60 votes when all 100 Senate seats are filled.

vocab.def: The course of action a government takes, or decides not to take, about a public problem.
vocab.example: A city decides to build larger storm drains to stop flooding.

notes:
Week 4 Study Sheet: Government in Action

Electoral votes = House members + 2 senators. D.C. = 3 (23rd Am.). Total 435 + 100 + 3 = 538. Majority to win = 270. Smallest state = 3. Winner-take-all in 48 states and D.C. No majority: the House picks from the top three, one vote per state delegation; 26 states needed (12th Am.).

Elections

  • Primary/caucus: picks each party's nominee (closed = party members only; open = any registered voter picks one ballot)
  • General election: Tuesday after the first Monday in November
  • House: 435, 2-year terms. Senate: 100, 6-year terms (1/3 every 2 years). President: 4 years, two-term limit (22nd Am.)
  • Census every 10 years: House seats and electoral votes shift
  • Popular vote winner lost: 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016

Party vs. Interest Group

  • Party: nominates candidates, writes a platform, organizes Congress, seeks control of government
  • Interest group: lobbies, testifies, petitions, advertises, sues, gives money through PACs
  • Test: nominates its own candidates? Yes = party. Endorsing or donating is not nominating.
  • Third parties rarely win (one winner per district) but spread ideas (Populists → 17th Am.)

How a Bill Becomes a Law

  1. Introduced by a member (revenue bills start in the House)
  2. Committee: hearings and markup (most bills die here)
  3. Floor vote: simple majority passes
  4. Other chamber passes the identical text (conference committee)
  5. President acts

Public Policy Stages and the Branches

Agenda setting (complaints, news) → Formulation (compare options) → Adoption (vote, sign) → Implementation (hire, build, enforce) → Evaluation (report results). Executive carries out laws (agencies write regulations, e.g., OSHA, 1970). Judicial reviews whether laws are constitutional (Marbury v. Madison, 1803). Legislative funds programs, holds oversight hearings; the Senate confirms nominees.
